title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
1 · What you hear → · Glossary
A piano note has a pitch you could hum and a drum’s thud has none because the piano’s frequencies sit, very nearly, on whole-number multiples of one frequency and the drum’s do not. This series explains where an instrument’s frequencies come from with one piece of mathematics: they are read off the spectrum of an operator, the rule in the instrument’s equation of motion. It works one instrument, the plucked string, completely, and then runs the same recipe on the others.

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
The posts

What you hear, with sounds and no differential equations: what makes a clear pitch, and what we hear as a sound’s pitch, loudness, timbre and duration. A clear pitch means the partials sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch, so the sound nearly repeats at that rate.
One string, end to end works the plucked string completely: where its equation comes from, from Newton’s law; why the sines are the right coordinates; why there is exactly one solution; how the motion becomes the sound; and which conditions it used. A plucked string moves as a sum of shapes \sin(n\pi x/L), each swinging at its own frequency nc/2L, because in the basis of sines, and only in a basis of eigenfunctions, the equation splits into independent springs.
Other instruments, same recipe runs the string’s recipe on a piano, a kalimba, a glockenspiel, drums, a bowed violin, a flute, a clarinet, a harmonica and a theremin, starting from an orchestra: a short entry for each, with its spectrum and its sound. Six deep dives work one instrument each in full, with the derivation of its equation: the violin, the clarinet, the kalimba, the harmonica, the piano and the drum.

Beyond. The appendix When does an equation have a spectrum? gives the general theory for mathematical readers: when the solution of a differential equation is a sum over the spectrum of an operator, the deeper theory, and counterexamples, smallest first. Two further posts take up questions the answers raise: Can you hear the shape of a drum? and Did instruments shape our scales?. A Piano is a playable upright with all 88 keys and its three pedals. Technical words link to the glossary.
Reading paths. In order, 1 → 2 → 3, since each post uses the one before it, then any of the six deep dives. A listener can read 1 → 3 and stop at the gallery, or open a deep dive such as the kalimba or the drum for one instrument; each links to the step of post 2 it reuses. A mathematician can read post 2, the deep dives for the derivations, then the appendix.

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
The series in one paragraph
An instrument left to ring sounds a sum of decaying pure tones, one per mode: 
p(t) = \sum_k a_k\, e^{-t/\tau_k} \cos(2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k).
 Here p(t) is the air pressure at the listener; partial k has frequency f_k, starting size a_k and phase \varphi_k, and shrinks by a factor of e \approx 2.7 every \tau_k seconds. This holds because a vibrating object of finite size whose motion is linear and unchanging in time moves, left to itself, as a sum of modes, shapes that each oscillate at their own frequency and fade at their own rate, apart from the special cases the appendix lists. The body, the air and the room pass that motion on in a way that is also linear and unchanging in time, which keeps every f_k and \tau_k, changes the amounts, and adds the filter’s own ringing (the body’s resonances, the room’s reverberation).
The equation of motion, through its operator together with friction and radiation, fixes where the partials sit and how fast they fade (the f_k, which the series derives, and the \tau_k, which are mostly measured); the playing, and where you listen, fix how strong they are, the a_k. Bowed and blown notes are different: their motion repeats one cycle, so their partials sit at exact whole-number multiples.

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
Operator families and instrument classes
The Hornbostel–Sachs classification, the scheme most used by those who study instruments, sorts them into five classes by what makes the sound;1 this series groups them instead by operator family: instruments whose operators agree up to constants and how they are held, so that one calculation covers them all. The decimal codes in the first column are the scheme’s.2
1 E. M. von Hornbostel and C. Sachs, “Systematik der Musikinstrumente: Ein Versuch”, Zeitschrift für Ethnologie 46 (1914), 553–590 (archive.org); fifth class added in C. DetailsThe decimal codes, and when electrophones were added

The numbers are the scheme’s decimal codes, read from the left (Wikipedia, Hornbostel–Sachs, and the infoboxes of the instruments’ articles). Among the chordophones (3), 321.322 are necked box lutes, such as the violin (bowed, 321.322-71) and the guitar; 322 are harps; 314.122 are board zithers with a resonator box, where the piano sits, as 314.122-4-8, sounded by hammers from a keyboard. Among the aerophones (4), 421.121.12 are open side-blown flutes with fingerholes; 422.211.2 are clarinets with a cylindrical bore and fingerholes; 412.132 are sets of free reeds, inside the interruptive free aerophones (412), where “the air-stream is interrupted periodically”. Among the idiophones (1), 122.1 are plucked idiophones in the form of a comb, with laced-on lamellae (thin tongues), and 111.222 are sets of struck percussion plaques. Among the membranophones (2), 211.11 are single kettle drums and 211.212.1 single cylindrical drums with two heads. Number 531.1 places the theremin in 53, Sachs’s group of radioelectric instruments, those that make their sound with electrically driven oscillators (Wikipedia, Electronic musical instrument; for electric oscillators other than the theremin’s coil and capacitor, Relaxation oscillator, Voltage-controlled oscillator and Hammond organ).
Hornbostel and Sachs published the scheme in 1914 with four classes (E. M. von Hornbostel and C. Sachs, “Systematik der Musikinstrumente: Ein Versuch”, Zeitschrift für Ethnologie 46 (1914), 553–590, archive.org); electrophones came later. Francis Galpin gave them a class of their own in his own scheme (F. W. Galpin, A Textbook of European Musical Instruments, 1937, pp. 27–36), and Sachs added them to Hornbostel–Sachs as a fifth class, with the groups 51 to 53 (C. Sachs, The History of Musical Instruments, Norton, New York, 1940, pp. 447–467). Anthony Baines and Klaus Wachsmann’s English translation keeps the four classes of 1914 (A. Baines and K. P. Wachsmann, “Classification of musical instruments”, The Galpin Society Journal 14 (1961), 3–29, doi:10.2307/842168; D. Lee, “Hornbostel-Sachs classification of musical instruments”, Knowledge Organization 47 (2020), 72–91, for the electrophones’ history and their absence from the translation).





DetailsWhat varies inside one operator family


Strings and air columns, -c^2\,d^2/dx^2. What moves, the string’s height or the air’s pressure; the constants that set the lowest frequency, such as length, tension and mass per length; the ends, which are part of the operator: tied, open at both ends (flute) or closed at one (clarinet, pan pipes); and the playing: plucked (guitar, harp), bowed (violin) or blown.
Bending bars, \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4. Steel tine, brass reed or metal bar; the ends, one clamped or both free, which change the frequency ratios; and the playing: plucked, struck or blown, which decides whether you hear the bar’s own overtones or the whole-number multiples of a steady airflow.
Stiff strings, -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4. The stiffness, whose effect is largest at the two ends of a piano’s keyboard (the piano in post 3).
Membranes, -c^2\Delta. Tension and size, and what surrounds the head, which matters for timpani.
A single number, such as s/m for a mass m on a spring of stiffness s or 1/LC for a coil and a capacitor (Wikipedia, LC circuit: Kirchhoff’s law and \omega = 1/\sqrt{LC}). Nothing varies but the number.






DetailsWhere the classes and the mathematics part ways

Hornbostel–Sachs asks what makes the sound; the operator asks what oscillates and by what rule. Mostly the answers line up. Where they part:

The piano is a chordophone, a board zither whose strings are struck by hammers, but its operator adds the bar’s fourth derivative to the string’s, -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4: its steel wire is stiff enough to bend like a bar (the piano in post 3).
The harmonica is an aerophone, classed by its interrupted airstream, though its reed is a clamped bar like the kalimba’s tine. That agrees with the harmonica in post 3: the steady sound has only whole-number multiples of the puff rate, set by the chopped airflow, and the reed’s own off-line overtones are absent from it.
The glockenspiel and the kalimba are idiophones in different groups, struck and plucked, and in one operator family. They share the rule \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, but their ends differ, both free for the glockenspiel bar and one clamped for the tine, so their operators differ, and so do their frequency ratios, 1 : 2.76 : 5.40 against 1 : 6.27 : 17.55.
A violin string and a flute’s air column are in different classes, yet their operators agree up to constants: both are -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 with the value held at zero at both ends, the string’s height at its tied ends and the air’s extra pressure at the flute’s open ends (post 3).
An electric guitar is a chordophone with a pickup: its strings make the sound, and the electronics only pick it up and amplify it (Wikipedia, Electric guitar).
A theremin is an electrophone: its two radio-frequency oscillators are coil-and-capacitor circuits, whose operator is the single number 1/LC, with the player’s hand as one plate of a capacitor and a mixer producing the audible difference (Wikipedia, Theremin); post 3 derives it.

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
Did instrument makers know?
Mostly not: makers found what works by trying and listening, and the theory explained it afterwards, often much later. Bell founders tuned each bell’s partials by ear and lathe for the Zutphen carillon of 1644,3 and experimenters found the laws of strings (Mersenne, 1636)4 and the still points of a vibrating string (Noble and Pigot in the 1670s; Sauveur, 1701).5 The wave equation (d’Alembert, 1747),6 modes and their superposition (Daniel Bernoulli, Euler, Fourier)7 and the spectral theory behind this series (Sturm and Liouville, Rayleigh, Hilbert, Weyl)8 came after. Designing an instrument by computing its spectrum before it is made is recent: computed marimba bar profiles appear around 1990,9 and a bell with a major third was designed by finite-element computation in the 1980s.10
3 Wikipedia, Jacob van Eyck and Zutphen.4 Wikipedia, Mersenne’s laws.5 J. Wallis, “Dr. Wallis’s Letter to the Publisher, Concerning a New Musical Discovery”, Philosophical Transactions 12 (1677) (JSTOR); S. Dostrovsky, “Sauveur, Joseph”, Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography.6 Wikipedia, Wave equation.7 Wikipedia, Daniel Bernoulli; MacTutor, Joseph Fourier.8 MacTutor, Charles Sturm, Lord Rayleigh and David Hilbert; Wikipedia, Weyl law.9 F. Orduña-Bustamante, “Nonuniform beams with harmonically related overtones for use in percussion instruments”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 90 (1991), 2935–2941 (doi:10.1121/1.401768).10 A. Schoofs, F. van Asperen, P. Maas and A. Lehr, “Computation of bell profiles using structural optimization”, Music Perception 4 (1987), 245–254 (doi:10.2307/40285368).


DetailsThe longer story, with sources

Instruments came first. How Antonio Stradivari made his violins is not documented, so saying that he worked by trial and ear is an inference (Wikipedia, Stradivarius). Bells show trial and ear at work more plainly. The blind Utrecht carillonneur Jacob van Eyck picked out the separate partials of a bell by whistling at them, and held that a bell must be tuned after casting by changing its shape. In 1644 the city of Zutphen ordered a carillon from the founders Pieter and François Hemony, with van Eyck as its adviser. The brothers cast the bells slightly too thick, turned each on a lathe and shaved metal from the inside until its five principal partials were in tune. The Zutphen carillon is counted as the first tuned carillon (Wikipedia, Jacob van Eyck, drawing on L. Rombouts, Singing Bronze: A History of Carillon Music, Leuven University Press, 2014, and B. Swager, A History of the Carillon, DMus thesis, Indiana University, 1993; Wikipedia, Zutphen).
Laws from experiment. The Pythagorean tradition tied consonant intervals to simple ratios of string lengths: half the length sounds an octave higher. In the late 1580s Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo’s father, hung weights on strings and found that tension works differently: an octave needs four times the weight and a fifth 9 : 4, so the frequency goes with the square root of the tension (“July 2, 1591: Death of Vincenzo Galilei”, APS News, July 2015, following S. Drake’s dating of the experiments to 1588; W. B. Ashworth Jr., “Vincenzo Galilei”, Scientist of the Day, Linda Hall Library, 2 July 2024). Marin Mersenne’s Harmonie universelle (1636) stated the laws of a string together: its frequency is inversely proportional to its length, proportional to the square root of its tension and inversely proportional to the square root of its mass per length, as in f_1 = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu} in post 2 (Wikipedia, Mersenne’s laws). In Oxford in the mid-1670s William Noble and Thomas Pigot found that a string can vibrate in parts with still points between them: small pieces of paper hung on the string stayed at rest at some points and trembled at others. John Wallis reported the discovery in the Philosophical Transactions in 1677 (J. Wallis, “Dr. Wallis’s Letter to the Publisher, Concerning a New Musical Discovery; Written from Oxford, March 14. 1676/7”, Philosophical Transactions 12 (1677), JSTOR; Wikipedia, Thomas Pigot). In 1701 Joseph Sauveur explained such motions to the Paris Academy: a string can vibrate at higher frequencies, which he called harmonics, separated by still points, which he called nodes; both words are still in use (S. Dostrovsky, “Sauveur, Joseph”, Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography).
The mathematics, after the fact. Brook Taylor (1713) worked out from mechanics the shape and the period of a string’s simplest vibration (MacTutor, Brook Taylor). Jean le Rond d’Alembert (1747) wrote down the wave equation and solved it as two waves running in opposite directions (Wikipedia, Wave equation). Daniel Bernoulli (1753) stated that the general motion of a vibrating system is a superposition of its modes; Euler, d’Alembert and Lagrange did not accept that sums of sines could match an arbitrary starting shape (Wikipedia, Daniel Bernoulli, quoting L. Brillouin, Wave Propagation in Periodic Structures, 1946, for the 1753 statement). Leonhard Euler worked out the vibrations of a drumhead (L. Euler, “De motu vibratorio tympanorum”, Novi Commentarii academiae scientiarum Petropolitanae 10 (1766), 243–260, Euler Archive, E302), and the functions now named after Bessel appear there for every whole-number order; the simplest, J_0, had already turned up in Daniel Bernoulli’s hanging chain in the 1730s (R. C. Archibald, “Mathematicians and music”, American Mathematical Monthly 31 (1924), 1–25, part 3 on MacTutor, which also covers Taylor and d’Alembert; Wikipedia, Bessel function, history; D. D. Nolte, “The ups and downs of the compound double pendulum”, Galileo Unbound, 2020, for the hanging chain). Ernst Chladni (1787) made the nodal lines of vibrating plates visible with sand (Wikipedia, Ernst Chladni). Joseph Fourier, in a memoir of 1807 and a book of 1822, argued that any function can be written as a sum of sines and cosines, and used such sums to solve the equation of heat flow (MacTutor, Joseph Fourier; Wikipedia, Fourier series). Charles Sturm and Joseph Liouville (1836–37) developed expansions of this kind for a whole class of second-order equations, the eigenvalue problems now named after them (MacTutor, Charles Sturm). Karl Weierstrass (1858) corrected a conclusion of Lagrange, repeated by Laplace and others: they had held that two equal frequencies would make a small oscillation grow with time, and Weierstrass showed that for small oscillations about a stable rest they do not (K. Weierstrass, “Über ein die homogenen Functionen zweiten Grades betreffendes Theorem, nebst Anwendung desselben auf die Theorie der kleinen Schwingungen”, Monatsberichte der Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin (1858), 207–220, reprint in Mathematische Werke 1; F. Brechenmacher, “L’identité algébrique d’une pratique portée par la discussion sur l’équation à l’aide de laquelle on détermine les inégalités séculaires des planètes (1766–1874)”, arXiv:0704.2931, which quotes Lagrange (1766) and Weierstrass’s correction). Lord Rayleigh’s The Theory of Sound (1877) gathered the subject into one treatise (MacTutor, Lord Rayleigh). David Hilbert’s work on integral equations in the 1900s introduced the name spectral theory (MacTutor, David Hilbert; Wikipedia, Spectral theory), and Hermann Weyl (1911) proved that the frequencies of a drum determine its area (Wikipedia, Weyl law; Can you hear the shape of a drum?).
Computed design is recent. A marimba bar is thinned by an arch cut under its middle. The arch lowers the lowest frequency more than the overtones, and so moves the first overtone from 2.76 times the lowest, the uniform bar of Did instruments shape our scales?, up to a whole-number multiple, usually 4 (N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 19). Makers such as J. C. Deagan’s company in Chicago, building marimbas from the early 1900s, and later Clair Omar Musser’s, tuned each bar by grinding the arch and checking the result, by ear and with pitch-measuring devices as they appeared, such as Deagan’s own “Deagan-o-meter” (1915) and the strobe tuner (1936); the shape of the arch was found by trial (Percussive Arts Society, Hall of Fame: John Calhoun Deagan; “Chicago shop plays key role in keeping world’s ensembles in tune”, WTTW News, 2016; Wikipedia, Clair Omar Musser and Electronic tuner, for the first strobe tuner, Conn, 1936). Bar profiles computed in advance, before any wood or metal is cut, appear in the acoustics literature around 1990 (F. Orduña-Bustamante, “Nonuniform beams with harmonically related overtones for use in percussion instruments”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 90 (1991), 2935–2941, doi:10.1121/1.401768). Bells followed the same path. A traditional tuned bell has a minor third among its main partials. In the 1980s engineers at the Eindhoven University of Technology designed a bell with a major third instead, by finite-element computation and structural optimization, and the Eijsbouts bell foundry cast it (A. Schoofs, F. van Asperen, P. Maas and A. Lehr, “Computation of bell profiles using structural optimization”, Music Perception 4 (1987), 245–254, doi:10.2307/40285368; Wikipedia, Bell, section “Major third bell”).

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← Beyond · When does an equation have a spectrum? · Beyond · Did instruments shape our scales? → · Glossary
All of a drum’s frequencies tell you its area and, for a reasonable rim, the length of its rim, but not always its shape: the two drums below have different shapes and exactly the same frequencies. Play each with every mode equally loud, then click a drum to strike it at a point.
The reason: Counting a drum’s frequencies reveals its area and its rim. But these two drums are cut from the same seven triangles so that every mode of one can be rebuilt on the other. In 1966 the mathematician Mark Kac asked whether a perfect ear could work out a drum’s shape from its frequencies;1 for drums in the plane the answer, found in 1992, is no.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
The drum’s spectrum
The frequencies of a drum are decided by its shape alone, apart from one overall factor. Let the drumhead be a region \Omega of the plane, in one piece, and u(x, y, t) the height of the head above the point (x, y) at time t. Newton’s law for a small patch of the head, pulled by the tension in its edges, gives (the drums in post 3) 
u_{tt} = c^2\,\Delta u \ \text{ inside } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \ \text{ on the rim},
 where \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy} is the Laplacian and c^2 is the tension divided by the mass per unit area. The Laplacian is positive where u sits below the average of u around it, and negative where it sits above, so each point of the head accelerates toward the average height around it. The model assumes, as in post 3, small slopes, a tension that is the same everywhere and does not change as the head moves, no bending stiffness, no air, and no damping.
In the series’ form u_{tt} = -A\,u, the operator is A = -c^2\Delta, acting on shapes that are zero on the rim; the rim condition is part of the operator. A mode is a shape X that A only rescales, AX = \lambda X. Writing \lambda = c^2k^2, 
-\Delta X = k^2 X \ \text{ inside } \Omega, \qquad X = 0 \ \text{ on the rim}.
 The numbers k^2 for which this has a solution other than X = 0 are the eigenvalues of -\Delta on \Omega, and the solutions are its eigenfunctions, the mode shapes; both depend only on \Omega. List the eigenvalues in order, k_1^2 \le k_2^2 \le \cdots, each repeated as often as it occurs (its multiplicity). Mode n has the operator’s eigenvalue \lambda_n = c^2k_n^2 and swings at 
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{c\,k_n}{2\pi}.

Kac’s question, precisely. Knowing c, hearing every frequency means knowing every k_n^2. Does the list k_1^2, k_2^2, \dots determine \Omega, up to sliding, turning or flipping the drum, which change no frequency? Kac wrote that he had first heard the question posed this way about ten years earlier, from Salomon Bochner.2
2 Kac, “Can one hear the shape of a drum?”, American Mathematical Monthly 73 (1966), part II, 1–23.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
Same frequencies, different sound
The two drums at the top share every frequency, but struck at a point they sound different. Their first twelve frequencies, as multiples of the lowest, k_n/k_1, are 1×, 1.20×, 1.43×, 1.60×, 1.69×, 1.90×, 2.04×, …, the same for both drums to every digit computed. Like the drum in post 3, they sit off the whole-number lines, so neither drum has a clear pitch.


  
  Both drums' first twelve frequencies, as multiples of the lowest, every mode drawn equally tall: drum A and drum B have exactly these stems. Values from T. A. Driscoll, Eigenmodes of isospectral drums, SIAM Review 39 (1997), Table 3.1.


A struck drum moves as a sum of its modes, 
u = \sum_n a_n X_n \cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n),
 so its sound is a sum of tones at the frequencies f_n, each fading at its own rate, with a strength a_n that depends on where it is struck; what you hear also depends on where you listen. The two drums share the f_n but not the mode shapes X_n, so a strike at a given point starts the modes with different strengths, and the timbre differs. Played with every a_n = 1, as the “every mode equal” buttons do, the two drums sound identical. What they share is the answer to “which frequencies can this drum make”, which is exactly what the spectrum records.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
What the spectrum knows
Counting the frequencies gives the area and the rim. Count the eigenvalues of -\Delta up to a limit \Lambda, N(\Lambda) = \#\{n : k_n^2 \le \Lambda\}, where \# means “the number of” (a frequency limit f corresponds to \Lambda = (2\pi f/c)^2). For a high limit, 
N(\Lambda) \approx \frac{|\Omega|}{4\pi}\,\Lambda \;-\; \frac{P}{4\pi}\sqrt{\Lambda},
 where |\Omega| is the drum’s area and P the length of its rim. The number of modes below a high limit grows in proportion to the area, so twice the area gives about twice as many modes; it falls short of the area’s share by an amount in proportion to the rim’s length, because holding the rim still costs the drum some modes.
The first term is Weyl’s law: Hermann Weyl proved it in 1911, and later work extended it to every drum,3 so the area can be heard. The second term is subtler. For the count itself it is proved only for some drums: Victor Ivrii proved it in 1980 for smooth rims on which closed billiard paths are rare (fold below).4 For a slightly smoothed version of the count it is proved for every drum whose rim is smooth or made of straight pieces, and that is enough to hear the rim’s length.5 Where the second term holds, “\approx” means that the error, divided by \sqrt\Lambda, shrinks to zero as \Lambda grows.
3 Wikipedia, Weyl law (Weyl 1911).4 Wikipedia, Weyl law (Ivrii 1980).5 Å. Pleijel, “A study of certain Green’s functions with applications in the theory of vibrating membranes”, Arkiv för Matematik 2 (1954), 553–569, for smooth rims; M. van den Berg and S. Srisatkunarajah, “Heat equation for a region in R² with a polygonal boundary”, Journal of the London Mathematical Society 37 (1988), 119–127, for polygons.The demo counts the modes of three drums with the same area. Once the area’s share, the same for all three, is taken away, the drum with the longest rim sits lowest.

  Three drums of equal area: a disk, a square, a long rectangle. Steps: the true counts. Dashed: Weyl's formula, area and rim together. Gray: the area's share alone, the same for all three.





PreciselyWhat the demo plots, and Ivrii’s condition on billiard paths limits

In the demo all three drums have area |\Omega| = \pi (a disk of radius 1, a square, and a rectangle 4 times as long as it is wide), so the area’s share is \Lambda/4, and “minus the area’s share” plots N(\Lambda) - \Lambda/4, roughly -P\sqrt\Lambda/4\pi: the longer the rim, the lower the curve. The demo’s frequency limit is shown as a multiple of the disk’s lowest frequency, \sqrt{\Lambda}/k_1.
Ivrii’s condition: a billiard path is the path of a ball rolling inside the drum and bouncing off the rim, angle in equal to angle out; it is closed if it comes back to where it started, heading the same way. “Rare” means that if you pick a starting point and a direction at random, the chance of landing on a closed path is zero. Ivrii conjectured that this always holds; it has not been proved (Wikipedia, Weyl law). The square and the rectangle in the demo have corners, which his theorem does not cover, but for them the formula can be checked by counting, as in the next fold. The perimeter can be heard in any case, for every drum whose rim is smooth or a polygon, by a smoother way of counting; that is the fold after it.





Proof sketchWeyl’s law for a square, by counting dots partial derivatives

Take the square of side s. Its eigenfunctions of -\Delta are \sin(m\pi x/s)\sin(n\pi y/s) for whole numbers m, n \ge 1, with eigenvalues k^2 = (\pi/s)^2(m^2 + n^2); substituting them into the equation checks this, as for the loop of string in the appendix. So N(\Lambda) is the number of dots (m, n), with m, n \ge 1, inside the quarter circle of radius R = s\sqrt\Lambda/\pi.















RR

Give each dot the unit square centered on it. These squares nearly fill the quarter disk, which has area \pi R^2/4. What they miss is a strip of width \tfrac12 along each axis, of area about R/2 each, shaded in the figure; the squares sticking out past the arc and the gaps inside it roughly cancel. So 
N(\Lambda) \approx \frac{\pi R^2}{4} - R = \frac{s^2}{4\pi}\Lambda - \frac{4s}{4\pi}\sqrt\Lambda = \frac{|\Omega|}{4\pi}\Lambda - \frac{P}{4\pi}\sqrt\Lambda .
 In the figure, R = 5.3: there are 17 dots, and the formula gives 16.8. The strips are missing because m = 0 and n = 0 give the zero function, not an eigenfunction: the rim’s condition u = 0 is what costs the perimeter term. Making “roughly cancel” precise is a classical problem about counting lattice points in a circle.





Proof sketchHearing the perimeter of a drum with a smooth or straight-sided rim: a smoother count the heat equation and a mirror-image trick

N(\Lambda) jumps by one at every eigenvalue, and those jumps can bunch up, which is what Ivrii’s condition controls. A smoother count avoids them. For t > 0 let 
Z(t) = \sum_n e^{-k_n^2 t}.
 Each eigenvalue adds nearly 1 if k_n^2 is much less than 1/t and nearly 0 if it is much more, so Z(t) is roughly N(1/t), with the jumps smoothed out. Like N, Z is determined by the list of eigenvalues.
Z has a physical meaning. Heat spreading on the drumhead, with the rim held at temperature 0, obeys v_t = \Delta v, the drum’s equation with one time derivative instead of two, so each mode now decays like e^{-k_n^2 t} instead of oscillating. Start a unit burst of heat at a point x and let it spread for time t. The temperature it leaves at x itself, added up over all points x of the drum, is Z(t). (Write the burst as a sum of modes, each scaled so that \iint X_n^2\,dA = 1. A burst at x contains mode n in proportion to X_n(x), the same rule as a strike on the drums in post 3; after time t that part has shrunk by e^{-k_n^2 t}, and its temperature at x is again proportional to X_n(x). So the temperature left at x is \sum_n e^{-k_n^2 t}X_n(x)^2, and adding it up over the drum gives \sum_n e^{-k_n^2 t}.) In a short time t heat travels a distance of about \sqrt t, so a burst only feels the rim if it starts within about that distance of it. Kac called this “not feeling the boundary”. Then:

Away from the rim, the burst spreads as on an endless plane, and the temperature it leaves at its starting point is 1/(4\pi t). Adding this up over the drum gives |\Omega|/(4\pi t).
Near a straight piece of rim, at distance r from it, the rim’s condition v = 0 is met by adding a mirror-image burst of opposite sign on the far side of the rim; a wave on a string meets a tied end the same way, as if an upside-down mirror image arrived from beyond it. The image is a distance 2r away, and lowers the temperature at x by e^{-r^2/t}/(4\pi t). Adding this up over a strip along the rim, using \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/t}\,dr = \tfrac12\sqrt{\pi t} for each unit of rim length, gives -P/(8\sqrt{\pi t}).

So, as t \to 0, 
Z(t) = \frac{|\Omega|}{4\pi t} - \frac{P}{8\sqrt{\pi t}} + (\text{terms that stay bounded}).
 Knowing Z, one reads off |\Omega| from the first term and then P from the second. Kac gave this argument in his 1966 paper (M. Kac, “Can one hear the shape of a drum?”, American Mathematical Monthly 73 (1966), part II, 1–23, MAA). Åke Pleijel had already proved the formula for smooth rims in 1954, by another method (Å. Pleijel, “A study of certain Green’s functions with applications in the theory of vibrating membranes”, Arkiv för Matematik 2 (1954), 553–569). Henry McKean and Isadore Singer proved in 1967 the next, constant term, which Kac had conjectured from an argument that was not a full proof: (1 - h)/6 for a drum with h holes and a smooth rim (H. P. McKean and I. M. Singer, “Curvature and the eigenvalues of the Laplacian”, Journal of Differential Geometry 1 (1967), 43–69). Michiel van den Berg and Sivakolundu Srisatkunarajah proved the formula for polygons in 1988 (M. van den Berg and S. Srisatkunarajah, “Heat equation for a region in R² with a polygonal boundary”, Journal of the London Mathematical Society 37 (1988), 119–127). Unlike N, Z needs no condition on billiard paths, because averaging over a range of eigenvalues smooths out the bunching.


So a round drum can be heard. Of all shapes with the same area, the disk has the shortest rim. This is the isoperimetric inequality: every drum satisfies 
P^2 \ge 4\pi\,|\Omega|,
 with equality only for the disk. Both sides can be heard, for a rim that is smooth or made of straight pieces. So a drum with such a rim that has exactly a disk’s frequencies has the disk’s area and rim length, so P^2 = 4\pi|\Omega|, so it is a disk. Kac pointed this out: “By pitch alone one can thus determine whether a drum is circular or not!”6
6 Kac, “Can one hear the shape of a drum?”, 1966, section 10.7 J. Milnor, “Eigenvalues of the Laplace operator on certain manifolds”, PNAS 51 (1964), 542.8 C. Gordon, D. Webb and S. Wolpert, “One cannot hear the shape of a drum”, Bulletin of the AMS 27 (1992), 134–138 (AMS, arXiv).But in general, no. Two years before Kac’s paper, John Milnor had found two different shapes with the same frequencies, and Kac said so; but they were 16-dimensional and had no rim.7 (They are flat tori: 16-dimensional versions of a video-game screen whose edges wrap around, so that leaving on the right brings you back on the left.) For drums in the plane the question stayed open for 26 years. In 1992 Carolyn Gordon, David Webb and Scott Wolpert found two different polygons with exactly the same frequencies, repeats included: the two drums at the top of this page.8 Such drums are called isospectral. Since area and rim length can be heard, they must share them, and they do: each is made of seven copies of the same right triangle, with two short sides of length 1, so each has area 3.5 and rim length 6 + 3\sqrt2.
They share every frequency because any mode of drum A can be rebuilt on drum B. Cut each drum into its seven triangles, and fill each of B’s triangles with three triangle-shaped pieces of the mode, taken from A’s triangles, turned or flipped to fit, some with their signs reversed. With the right choice of pieces and signs, they join smoothly across every seam and stay still on B’s rim, so the result is a mode of B at the same frequency.9 The construction runs backwards too, so the two drums have exactly the same frequencies, with the same number of modes at each.
9 P. Buser, J. Conway, P. Doyle and K.-D. Semmler, “Some planar isospectral domains”, International Mathematics Research Notices 1994, 391–400 (arXiv); C. Moler, “Can one hear the shape of a drum? Part 3, transplantation”, MathWorks, 2012.


DetailsTransplantation: carrying a mode from one drum to the other the Laplacian (post 3)

Cut each drum along its seams into its seven triangles. Take any eigenfunction X of drum A, with -\Delta X = k^2 X. On each triangle of drum B, place a sum of three pieces of X, each taken from one of A’s triangles, turned or reflected to fit, and some with a minus sign. Each piece satisfies -\Delta X = k^2 X, so the sum does too, inside each triangle. With the right choice of pieces and signs, the result is zero on B’s rim, and across every seam of B both its values and its slopes match. A function that satisfies the equation on both sides of a line, with values and slopes matching on the line, satisfies it across the line too, a standard fact about this equation. At the points where several seams meet, one more standard fact closes the gap: a solution that stays bounded around a single point, and satisfies the equation everywhere near it except possibly at the point itself, satisfies it there too. So the result is an eigenfunction of B with the same k^2, and so the same frequency. The construction can be reversed, so each eigenvalue has the same multiplicity on both drums.
This argument is called transplantation. It grew out of work of Peter Buser on surfaces in the 1980s and of Pierre Bérard around 1992 (P. Bérard, “Transplantation et isospectralité I”, Mathematische Annalen 292 (1992), 547–559); the version for drums like these is in a 1994 paper of Buser, John Conway, Peter Doyle and Klaus-Dieter Semmler (P. Buser, J. Conway, P. Doyle and K.-D. Semmler, “Some planar isospectral domains”, International Mathematics Research Notices 1994, 391–400, arXiv). The seven formulas, with pictures, are in Cleve Moler’s blog post (C. Moler, “Can one hear the shape of a drum? Part 3, transplantation”, Cleve’s Corner, MathWorks, August 2012), and in S. J. Chapman’s article, which does the same by folding paper (S. J. Chapman, “Drums that sound the same”, American Mathematical Monthly 102 (1995), 124–138). Gordon, Webb and Wolpert’s own proof used a method of Toshikazu Sunada for building isospectral spaces from group theory (T. Sunada, “Riemannian coverings and isospectral manifolds”, Annals of Mathematics 121 (1985), 169–186); Wikipedia, Hearing the shape of a drum, has an overview.





DetailsHow the numbers on this page were computed matrices, as for the beads in post 2

Each drum is covered by a square grid of spacing h, and the Laplacian is replaced by its five-point version: at each grid point, the sum of the four neighbors minus four times the point, divided by h^2. This is the bead model of post 2 in two dimensions. Grid points on the rim are held at zero. The drums’ corners sit on grid points, so whether each point is inside, on the rim, or outside is decided with exact whole-number arithmetic.
At h = 1/40 and h = 1/80 the two drums give the same first twelve eigenvalues k_n^2 of -\Delta to a relative difference of 3\times10^{-14}, which is rounding error. This is expected, as far as I can tell, because the grid lines up with every triangle’s edges, so transplantation works for the grid model too; Moler’s post transplants grid eigenvectors in the same way (C. Moler, “Part 2, eigenfunctions”, Cleve’s Corner, 2012). Combining the two grids (Richardson extrapolation) gives values within 0.03% of the high-accuracy values in Table 3.1 of Driscoll’s paper, after multiplying his by 4: his drums are twice the size of these (T. A. Driscoll, “Eigenmodes of isospectral drums”, SIAM Review 39 (1997), 1–17, DOI, PDF). That is a check, not a precise computation: Richardson’s trick assumes the grid error shrinks like h^2, and the drums’ inward-pointing corners slow that down. The page uses Driscoll’s values.
One eigenvalue is known exactly, the ninth, k_9^2. Its mode is, on each triangle, that triangle’s own lowest mode, \sin\pi x\,\sin 2\pi y - \sin 2\pi x\,\sin\pi y in coordinates where the triangle has corners (0,0), (1,0) and (1,1), with its sign flipping across each seam. Substituting gives k_9^2 = \pi^2(1 + 4) = 5\pi^2 = 49.348\ldots, and Driscoll’s value agrees to every digit he gives. On the grid, the ninth eigenvalue equals the grid version of this mode’s eigenvalue to rounding error, a second check.
The scripts are gww.py for the eigenvalues and gww_modes.py for the mode pictures. The corner coordinates are those in Moler’s first post (C. Moler, “Part 1, eigenvalues”, Cleve’s Corner, 2012). The mode pictures use the coarser grid h = 1/40, sampled every 0.1.


The study of what a spectrum says about the shape behind it is called spectral geometry.

title: When does an equation have a spectrum?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← 3 · Other instruments, same recipe · Beyond · Can you hear the shape of a drum? → · Glossary
A linear equation U' = BU that does not change in time has as its solutions exactly the combinations of modes e^{st}W when, and only when, B has a basis of eigenvectors. The free vibration of a stable, frictionless object of finite size, u'' = -Au with A self-adjoint, positive and with compact resolvent, always passes once any rigid drifts (\lambda = 0) are split off, with frequencies \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi for the eigenvalues \lambda of A. This page works up to that from the smallest examples, then gives the theory behind it, the smallest examples where it fails, and how it connects back to what we hear.
The reason, in one sentence: for a linear equation that does not change in time, the time derivative of a solution is again a solution, so there are solutions e^{st}W that differentiation only rescales, and these are enough exactly when the vectors W form a basis.

title: When does an equation have a spectrum?
text:
Recap: the equation of motion
For an object held in a given way, the operator A is the linear map, defined on the shapes the holding allows, that sends a shape to minus the acceleration it causes, and Newton’s law for small motions reads u'' = -A\,u, with u(t) the shape at time t and primes time derivatives. As in the rest of the series, A includes its constants, \lambda is an eigenvalue of A and f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi: a mass m on a spring of stiffness s has A = s/m and one mode. Post 2’s two beads, of mass m on a string of tension T, spaced h apart and h from the tied ends, have A = \frac{T}{mh}\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right), with eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, -1) and eigenvalues T/mh and 3T/mh: the sum S = u_1 + u_2 and the difference D = u_1 - u_2 swing as independent springs, with frequencies in the ratio 1 : \sqrt3.

title: When does an equation have a spectrum?
text:
The smallest examples
Two variations on post 2’s beads and string show what is new: closing the beads into a ring gives a motion that is not a combination of modes, and closing the string into a loop puts its frequencies exactly on the whole numbers.

  
  
  
  
  u₁u₂ends tied
  
  
  12closed into a ring

The two-bead ring: a drift. Join the string’s ends to each other and each bead has the other as its neighbor on both sides: A_{\text{ring}} = \frac{T}{mh}\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right), a different operator for the same beads. Now A_{\text{ring}}(1, 1) = 0: both beads move up together and nothing pulls back. Started moving, it drifts away silently, u = (1, 1)(a + bt). The other eigenvalue is 4T/mh.


  
    
    
  
  
    Together, S
    Opposite, D
    A mix
     close into a ring
    Hear this motion
  
  Slowed down. Tied ends: S swings at 1×, D at 1.73× (√3). Closed into a ring: nothing pulls S back; started at rest, it just stays shifted (a constant displacement), and D swings at 2×. On the right, the plane of the two heights (u₁ across, u₂ up): the path of a mix is a tangle, while S and D each run straight along their own tilted line. The model has no friction; the sound, with S at 196 Hz, fades only so that it stops.


The loop of string: exactly on the whole numbers. Join a continuous string into a loop, and measure position by the angle \theta, in units where the circumference is 2\pi. Post 2’s string equation becomes 
u_{tt} = -A\,u, \qquad A = -c^2\,\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu},
 on shapes that close up after one turn, X(\theta + 2\pi) = X(\theta); subscripts are partial derivatives. A mode’s shape satisfies AX = \lambda X, that is, X'' = -(\lambda/c^2)\,X (primes in \theta). For \lambda = c^2k^2 > 0 (here k is a wavenumber), X = a\cos k\theta + b\sin k\theta, which closes up exactly when k is a whole number n. For \lambda = 0, X = a + b\theta closes up only if b = 0: the whole loop lifted, no sound. No \lambda is negative (fold). So mode n, with eigenfunctions \cos n\theta and \sin n\theta, sounds at 
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{nc}{2\pi} = n\,f_1 ,
 exactly a whole-number multiple of the lowest, for two reasons. Each wave has a whole number of crests, because it must close up. And every wave travels at the same speed: u = g(\theta - ct) solves the equation for every shape g, since u_{tt} and c^2u_{\theta\theta} both equal c^2g''. Mode n is two such waves running in opposite directions, \cos n\theta\cos nct = \tfrac12\cos n(\theta - ct) + \tfrac12\cos n(\theta + ct), whose n crests pass a fixed point n times while one crest goes around. On beads short waves are slower, on a stiff piano wire faster; both leave the whole numbers.


  
  Beads
  
  
  Hear the first modes together
  A ring of beads with the loop's size, tension and total mass, the mass shared among more and more beads. Stems: the first ten frequencies, as multiples of the lowest; the slider's last position is the continuous loop, where every stem sits on its line. Higher modes are drawn and played quieter, so they are not shrill; the lowest plays at 196 Hz.


Every shape is a sum of these waves,1 its Fourier series f(\theta) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n\ge1}(a_n\cos n\theta + b_n\sin n\theta) (the amounts, and in what sense, in the fold). Released from rest, each wave swings at its own frequency, u(\theta, t) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_n (a_n\cos n\theta + b_n\sin n\theta)\cos(nct), so the motion repeats every 2\pi/c, and so does its sound (post 1).
1 E. M. Stein and R. Shakarchi, Fourier Analysis: An Introduction, Princeton University Press, 2003, chapters 1–3; Wikipedia, Fourier series.


PreciselyNo negative eigenvalues, and in what sense every shape is a sum of waves uses complex numbers and analysis

No negative eigenvalue. If X'' = qX with q > 0 on the loop, multiply by X and integrate over one turn. Integration by parts, with no boundary terms on a closed loop, gives \int X''X\,d\theta = -\int (X')^2\,d\theta \le 0, while q\int X^2\,d\theta \ge 0. Both are then zero, so X = 0.
The amounts. For a shape f of the loop, 
\begin{gathered}
f(\theta) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos n\theta + b_n\sin n\theta\big), \\
a_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f\cos n\theta\,d\theta, \qquad b_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f\sin n\theta\,d\theta .
\end{gathered}
 The amounts come from perpendicularity: \int_0^{2\pi}\cos n\theta\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0 for n \ne m, likewise for sines and for a sine against a cosine, so multiplying by \cos m\theta and integrating leaves \pi a_m. Whether every shape, a plucked corner included, is such a sum was argued over from the 1740s by d’Alembert, Euler and Daniel Bernoulli and settled much later (J. O. Smith III, Daniel Bernoulli’s modal decomposition, CCRMA, Stanford; Wikipedia, Fourier series).
The series. With Euler’s formula e^{in\theta} = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta, the series reads f = \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z} c_n e^{in\theta} with c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f e^{-in\theta}\,d\theta, so c_{\pm n} = (a_n \mp i b_n)/2 for n \ge 1 and c_0 = a_0/2. The functions e^{in\theta}/\sqrt{2\pi} form an orthonormal basis of L^2(S^1), the functions on the circle with \int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta finite, for the inner product \langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi} f\bar g\,d\theta: for every f in L^2(S^1), 
\Big\| f - \sum_{|n|\le M} c_n e^{in\theta}\Big\| \to 0 \quad (M \to \infty), \qquad \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta = \sum_n |c_n|^2 ,
 the second identity being Parseval’s. Perpendicularity is the easy half. Completeness, that no nonzero f is perpendicular to every e^{in\theta}, is the real content: trigonometric sums approximate every continuous periodic function uniformly (Fejér’s theorem), and continuous functions are dense in L^2 (E. M. Stein and R. Shakarchi, Fourier Analysis: An Introduction, Princeton University Press, 2003, chapters 1–3).
At single points. Some continuous functions have Fourier series that diverge at a point, and Carleson proved in 1966 that the series of every L^2 function converges at almost every point. For shapes that are continuous and made of straight pieces it converges at every point (Dirichlet, 1829); the plucked triangle’s coefficients shrink like 1/n^2, which is why a few terms already look right in the demo below.


Build a plucked shape out of waves, then let it go:
