  The loop is cut open and laid flat; its two edges are the same point. Dashed: the exact motion (once let go, the bump splits into two half-height copies that travel apart). Solid: the sum of the waves so far, each swinging at its own frequency. The sound adds those waves at the plucked point, the lowest at 196 Hz, faded only so that it stops.

title: When does an equation have a spectrum?
section: Why an equation that doesn’t change in time has modes
text:
Why an equation that doesn’t change in time has modes
Why do such combinations exist? Three steps, for the two beads first.
1. The derivative of a solution is again a solution. Differentiate x'' = -Ax once in time. Because A doesn’t change with time, (x')'' = -A\,x': the velocity obeys the same equation. In pictures: a solution shifted in time, x(t + h), is a solution; by linearity so is (x(t + h) - x(t))/h, which becomes x' as h \to 0. Both ingredients matter: if A changed with time, differentiating would add -A'x, and the derivative of a nonlinear force on x is not the force on x'.
2. Look for a solution whose derivative is a multiple of itself, x' = s\,x for one number s. Then (e^{-st}x)' = 0, so x(t) = e^{st}X for a fixed column X.
3. Substitute. For x = e^{st}X, the equation x'' = -Ax reads s^2e^{st}X = -e^{st}AX, so 
A\,X = -s^2\,X :
 X is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue \lambda = -s^2. For the beads \lambda > 0, so s = \pm i\sqrt{\lambda} is imaginary, and by Euler’s formula, e^{i\omega t} = \cos\omega t + i\sin\omega t, the real part of e^{i\omega t}X is \cos(\omega t)\,X: the shape X swinging at angular frequency \omega = \sqrt{\lambda}. Two eigenvectors and two signs give four modes, as many as the numbers it takes to start two beads.
Every such equation, in one form. Collect the shape and its velocity into one state U = (u, u'). Then u'' = -Au becomes 
U' = B\,U, \qquad B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & I \\ -A & 0 \end{pmatrix},
 with I the identity (friction adds a term to the second row; see the three levels). Call B the equation’s generator: it turns the state into its rate of change. The same steps apply: U' is a solution whenever U is, and U = e^{st}W is one exactly when BW = sW.

Definition 1 (mode). For a linear system U' = BU with B constant: a nonzero solution U(t) = e^{st}W, i.e. BW = sW. If s is not real, its frequency is |\operatorname{Im} s|/2\pi and it fades at rate -\operatorname{Re} s; real motions are real parts, pairing s with its complex conjugate.

When \operatorname{Re} s < 0, the mode shrinks by the factor e in its fading time \tau = -1/\operatorname{Re} s. The swing of step 3 has its own, older name.2
2 Wikipedia, Normal mode.
Definition 2 (normal mode). For u'' = -Au: a real solution u(t) = \cos(\omega t + \varphi)\,X with X \ne 0 and \omega > 0. It exists if and only if AX = \omega^2X.

How the two definitions meet. Write u'' = -Au as U' = BU with U = (u, u') and B as above. A normal mode with \omega > 0 is the real part of the pair of Definition-1 modes s = \pm i\omega, W = (X, \pm i\omega X). At \omega = 0 the pair collapses into a Jordan block, the smallest way for a matrix to lack eigenvectors (B sends (0, X) to (X, 0) and that to zero): the rigid drift X(a + bt), b \ne 0, is a solution but not a mode (a constant displacement X is an s = 0 mode). In finite dimensions B is diagonalizable, that is, has a basis of eigenvectors, exactly when A is diagonalizable and invertible.



ProofNormal modes, drifts, and when B has a basis of eigenvectors uses linear algebra

Definition 2’s condition. For u = \cos(\omega t + \varphi)X, u'' = -\omega^2\cos(\omega t + \varphi)X and -Au = -\cos(\omega t + \varphi)AX. These agree for all t if and only if AX = \omega^2X: if they agree, take a t with \cos(\omega t + \varphi) \ne 0 and divide; the converse is the computation itself.
Eigenvectors of B. Let W = (X, Y). Then BW = sW says Y = sX and -AX = sY, that is, W = (X, sX) with AX = -s^2X and X \neq 0. So each eigenvalue \lambda of A gives the eigenvalues s of B with s^2 = -\lambda: two of them, \pm\sqrt{-\lambda}, when \lambda \neq 0 (for \lambda = \omega^2 > 0, s = \pm i\omega), and only s = 0 when \lambda = 0. The eigenvectors of B for s are the (X, sX) with X in A’s eigenspace for \lambda = -s^2.
The real part of the pair. With W_\pm = (X, \pm i\omega X), \tfrac12\big(e^{i\varphi}e^{i\omega t}W_+ + e^{-i\varphi}e^{-i\omega t}W_-\big) = \big(\cos(\omega t + \varphi)X,\ -\omega\sin(\omega t + \varphi)X\big), which equals \operatorname{Re}\big(e^{i(\omega t + \varphi)}W_+\big) and is the state (u, u') of the normal mode.
The drift. If AX = 0 with X \ne 0, then B(X, 0) = (0, 0) and B(0, X) = (X, 0). The solution starting at (aX, bX) is (X(a + bt), bX), as differentiating checks. The only eigenvectors of B in the span of (X, 0) and (0, X) are the multiples of (X, 0), so for b \neq 0 this solution is not a combination of modes.
Counting. Work over the complex numbers, with A of size n, and let g_\lambda be the dimension of A’s eigenspace for \lambda. By the second paragraph, and since eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are independent, B, of size 2n, has exactly 2\sum_{\lambda\ne0} g_\lambda + g_0 independent eigenvectors. Since \sum_\lambda g_\lambda \le n, with equality exactly when A is diagonalizable, this is at most 2(n - g_0) + g_0 = 2n - g_0, and it equals 2n exactly when g_0 = 0 (A invertible) and \sum_\lambda g_\lambda = n (A diagonalizable).


How much this guarantees. In finite dimensions, at least one mode: BW = sW has a solution W \ne 0 exactly when the polynomial \det(B - s) (the determinant, a polynomial in s whose roots are the eigenvalues) vanishes, and every polynomial has a complex root. One mode is not a basis: x'' = 0 has only one (counterexample 1). In infinite dimensions there may be none: on an infinite string the solutions e^{\pm ikx} of -c^2X'' = \lambda X have infinite energy, so none is an allowed shape.

title: When does an equation have a spectrum?
text:
The criterion
When are the modes enough for every motion? In words (precise statement and proof in the fold):

The criterion. The solutions of an equation are exactly all combinations of a fixed set of modes, with any amounts, when and only when the equation is linear, unchanging in time, and its generator has a full set of eigenvectors.

Checked on the two beads. Their A has the eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, -1) with the positive eigenvalues \lambda_1 = T/mh and \lambda_2 = 3T/mh, so it is diagonalizable and invertible, and B has the full set of four eigenvectors (X, \pm i\omega X), for s = \pm i\omega_1, \pm i\omega_2. So the solutions are exactly the combinations of these four modes with any amounts; in real form, 
x(t) = \begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}\big(a_1\cos\omega_1 t + b_1\sin\omega_1 t\big) + \begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\big(a_2\cos\omega_2 t + b_2\sin\omega_2 t\big), \qquad \omega_k = \sqrt{\lambda_k},
 with any four real numbers, which the starting heights and velocities fix. On the two-bead ring the criterion fails: A_{\text{ring}} has the eigenvalue 0, so B has only three independent eigenvectors, and the drift (1, 1)(a + bt), b \neq 0, is a solution no combination of modes produces. Split it off, as the opening statement does, and the rest passes.

Definition 3 (modal system). One whose modes form a basis of its states: every state is uniquely a (convergent) combination of mode vectors. (Infinite dimensions: a Riesz basis of the energy space, not merely a complete set.)

The two tied beads are modal; the two-bead ring is not. The deeper theory explains the Riesz basis.



ProofThe criterion as an equality of sets uses linear algebra

Statement. Let F: \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}^n, and call a differentiable U: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}^n a solution of U' = F(U) if U'(t) = F(U(t)) for every t. Let W_1, \dots, W_n be a basis of \mathbb{C}^n, let s_1, \dots, s_n be complex numbers, and let W be the matrix with columns W_k. Then the solutions of U' = F(U) are exactly all combinations 
U(t) = \sum_{k=1}^n c_k\,e^{s_k t}\,W_k ,
 with every coefficient vector c = (c_1, \dots, c_n) \in \mathbb{C}^n allowed, if and only if F(U) = BU for every U, with B = W\operatorname{diag}(s)\,W^{-1}.
Proof of “if”. Suppose F(U) = BU with B = W\operatorname{diag}(s)W^{-1}. Then BW = W\operatorname{diag}(s), which says BW_k = s_kW_k for each k. For any c, the function U(t) = \sum_k c_ke^{s_kt}W_k has U'(t) = \sum_k c_ks_ke^{s_kt}W_k = \sum_k c_ke^{s_kt}BW_k = BU(t), so it is a solution. Conversely, let U be any solution, and set c = W^{-1}U(0) and V(t) = \sum_k c_ke^{s_kt}W_k, a solution with V(0) = U(0). The difference Z = W^{-1}(U - V) satisfies Z' = W^{-1}B(U - V) = \operatorname{diag}(s)Z, so each entry obeys z_k' = s_kz_k; then (e^{-s_kt}z_k)' = 0, so z_k(t) = e^{s_kt}z_k(0) = 0. Hence U = V.
Proof of “only if”. Suppose the solutions are exactly the combinations, every c allowed. Take any vector Y \in \mathbb{C}^n and choose c = W^{-1}Y, which is allowed. The solution U(t) = \sum_kc_ke^{s_kt}W_k has U(0) = Wc = Y and U'(0) = \sum_kc_ks_kW_k = W\operatorname{diag}(s)\,c = W\operatorname{diag}(s)W^{-1}Y. Because U is a solution, U'(0) = F(U(0)) = F(Y). So F(Y) = W\operatorname{diag}(s)W^{-1}Y for every Y: the equation at time 0, applied to solutions starting at every state, forces F to be this linear map.
Remarks. (1) The same argument at any time t_0 in place of 0 shows that even an equation allowed to change in time, U' = F(t, U), whose solutions are exactly these combinations must have F(t, U) = BU for every t: linearity and time-invariance both follow, as the criterion in words says. (2) For a real equation, such as u'' = -Au with A real, the real solutions are those whose coefficients pair each mode with its complex conjugate, c_k with \bar c_k. (3) For continuous objects the same holds with a Riesz basis of the energy space in place of a basis, and square-summable coefficients (see the deeper theory below).





PreciselyWhy “with any amounts” matters uses derivatives

Exponentials with fixed exponents alone do not force an equation to be linear. On the half-line U > -\tfrac14, take 
U' = 2U - \frac{\sqrt{1 + 4U} - 1}{2} ,
 whose right side is smooth there. Every solution is 
U(t) = c\,e^{t} + c^2\,e^{2t}
 for one real number c, for as long as it stays in U > -\tfrac14: for c \ge 0 that is all t, and for c < 0 the solution reaches the edge U = -\tfrac14 when c\,e^t = -\tfrac12.
Proof. Put w = (\sqrt{1 + 4U} - 1)/2, which maps U > -\tfrac14 one-to-one onto w > -\tfrac12, with inverse U = w^2 + w. In terms of w the equation reads (2w + 1)\,w' = 2(w^2 + w) - w = w\,(2w + 1). Since 2w + 1 > 0, this is w' = w, so w = c\,e^t, and U = w^2 + w = c\,e^t + c^2e^{2t}, valid while c\,e^t > -\tfrac12.
Every solution is built from the same two exponentials, e^t and e^{2t}, yet the equation is not linear: the coefficients are tied, the second always the square of the first, and the sum of two solutions, (c + d)e^t + (c^2 + d^2)e^{2t}, is not a solution unless cd = 0. In the criterion, “every coefficient vector allowed” rules this out.

title: When does an equation have a spectrum?
section: Three levels, from the familiar to the general
text:
Three levels, from the familiar to the general
Three nested classes of equations, each with its exact condition: level 1 gives pure tones, level 2 adds fading, level 3 adds shapes whose parts lag behind one another.

Level 1 · Free vibration without friction
The equation is u'' = -Au with A self-adjoint and positive: pure tones at \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi, energy conserved. For beads, self-adjoint means symmetric, entry (i, j) equal to entry (j, i), and positive, A > 0, means x\cdot Ax > 0 for every x \ne 0.

Result (level 1, any number of beads). Let A be a real symmetric n\times n matrix with A > 0.

A has eigenvectors X_1, \dots, X_n forming an orthonormal basis (perpendicular, each of length 1), with eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n > 0.
Every solution of x'' = -Ax is 
x(t) = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\Big(a_i\cos\omega_i t + \frac{b_i}{\omega_i}\sin\omega_i t\Big), \qquad \omega_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i},
 with a_i = X_i\cdot x(0) and b_i = X_i\cdot x'(0): mode i sounds at f_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}/2\pi.
The energy E = \tfrac12\,x'\cdot x' + \tfrac12\,x\cdot Ax is the same at every moment.





ProofLevel 1 for any number of beads, and where symmetry comes from uses linear algebra

Part 1 is the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices; \lambda_i = X_i\cdot AX_i > 0 because A > 0.
For part 2, write x(t) = \sum_j c_j(t)X_j with c_j = X_j\cdot x, the amount of X_j in x. Take the dot product of x'' = -Ax with X_i. On the left, X_i\cdot x'' = c_i''. On the right, X_i\cdot Ax = (AX_i)\cdot x, because both sides equal \sum_{j,k}(X_i)_jA_{jk}x_k once A_{jk} = A_{kj}; so X_i\cdot Ax = \lambda_iX_i\cdot x = \lambda_ic_i. Hence c_i'' = -\lambda_ic_i for each i separately: n independent springs. Each has exactly one solution with c_i(0) = a_i and c_i'(0) = b_i, namely a_i\cos\omega_it + (b_i/\omega_i)\sin\omega_it (uniqueness as in the criterion’s proof).
For part 3, E' = x'\cdot x'' + \tfrac12(x'\cdot Ax + x\cdot Ax') = x'\cdot(x'' + Ax) = 0, using x\cdot Ax' = x'\cdot Ax for symmetric A.
Drifts. If A is symmetric with A \ge 0 and has the eigenvalue 0, its eigenvectors for 0 (the drifts) are perpendicular to the others, and A maps the perpendicular complement of the drifts to itself and is positive there. The motion splits accordingly: along each drift X, c'' = 0, so c = a + bt; on the rest, the result above.
Symmetry from energy. Near rest the stored energy is V(x) \approx \tfrac12\,x\cdot Kx, where the stiffness matrix K is the matrix of second derivatives of V, symmetric because mixed partial derivatives don’t depend on the order of differentiation. The restoring force is -\nabla V \approx -Kx, keeping the first-order term; that is where linearity comes from. A stable rest means x\cdot Kx > 0 except along rigid drifts.
Unequal masses. Newton’s law reads Mx'' = -Kx with M the diagonal matrix of masses, and A = M^{-1}K is symmetric in the mass-weighted dot product \sum_i m_ix_iy_i; equivalently v = M^{1/2}x obeys v'' = -M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}v with a symmetric matrix.


Why the instruments qualify. Symmetry: a stretch of string feels only the difference of its two beads’ heights, so bead j pulls bead i as hard as i pulls j. Positivity: displacing a held object stores energy. A shape storing none is a rigid drift, \lambda = 0, moving as X(a + bt); it is split off. For strings, tubes, bars and drums, with \langle f, g\rangle = \int f\,g, integration by parts gives symmetry and positivity (fold); that every shape is a sum of modes needs finiteness (the deeper theory).



ProofSymmetry and energy for strings, bars and drums uses integration by parts

For the string with tied ends, integrate by parts once: 
\langle Af, g\rangle = -c^2\int_0^L f''\,g\,dx = -c^2\big[f'\,g\big]_0^L + c^2\int_0^L f'\,g'\,dx = c^2\int_0^L f'\,g'\,dx ,
 since g(0) = g(L) = 0. The last expression does not change when f and g swap, so \langle Af, g\rangle = \langle f, Ag\rangle, and with g = f it is c^2\int (f')^2 \ge 0, zero only for a constant shape, which a tied end forbids. The bracket also vanishes on a loop and at a closed tube end, where f' = 0. For a bar, integrating by parts twice gives \kappa^2\int f''g''\,dx, every boundary term killed by clamped, pinned or free ends; for a drumhead, the two-dimensional version gives c^2\iint\nabla f\cdot\nabla g\,dA, the rim term killed by the fixed rim.
Two consequences follow as for matrices. Modes with different eigenvalues are perpendicular: if AX = \lambda X and AY = \mu Y, then \lambda\langle X, Y\rangle = \langle AX, Y\rangle = \langle X, AY\rangle = \mu\langle X, Y\rangle. And energy is conserved: with E = \tfrac12\langle u_t, u_t\rangle + \tfrac12\langle Au, u\rangle, symmetry gives E' = \langle u_t, u_{tt} + Au\rangle = 0; times the mass per unit length, the two terms are the kinetic energy and the energy stored in the stretched string, \tfrac12T\int u_x^2\,dx.




Level 2 · Friction that the same shapes split
The equation is 
u'' + C\,u' + A\,u = 0 ,
 with the friction C symmetric and commuting with A: AC = CA, that is, applying C then A gives the same as A then C. For example C = \alpha + \beta A (numbers \alpha, \beta; \alpha stands for \alpha I). In general, for unequal masses, Mu'' + Cu' + Ku = 0, the condition is CM^{-1}K = KM^{-1}C.3 The standing shapes stay real, and each fades.
3 T. K. Caughey and M. E. J. O’Kelly, “Classical normal modes in damped linear dynamic systems”, Journal of Applied Mechanics 32 (1965), 583–588.
Result (level 2). Let A and C be real symmetric n\times n matrices with AC = CA.

There is an orthonormal basis X_1, \dots, X_n of shared eigenvectors: AX_k = \lambda_kX_k and CX_k = \gamma_kX_k.
Every solution of u'' + Cu' + Au = 0 is u(t) = \sum_k q_k(t)X_k, where each amount obeys its own equation, q_k'' + \gamma_kq_k' + \lambda_kq_k = 0.
The system is modal exactly when, for every shared eigenvector (with values \lambda for A and \gamma for C), s^2 + \gamma s + \lambda = 0 has distinct roots.

For light friction, \gamma_k^2 < 4\lambda_k, mode k is the real shape X_k swinging at f_k = \sqrt{\lambda_k - \gamma_k^2/4}\,/2\pi and fading with the time \tau_k = 2/\gamma_k.

Critical damping of one mode, \gamma^2 = 4\lambda, breaks it: the roots coincide, and that mode moves as (a + bt)e^{-\gamma t/2}, which no combination of modes produces (counterexample 2).



ProofLevel 2 uses linear algebra

Part 1. Each eigenspace E_\lambda of A is mapped to itself by C: if AX = \lambda X then A(CX) = CAX = \lambda\,CX. On E_\lambda, C is symmetric, so E_\lambda has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of C. Together over all \lambda these give part 1, since the eigenspaces of A are perpendicular and fill out \mathbb{R}^n.
Part 2. Take the dot product of the equation with X_k and use symmetry as in level 1: X_k\cdot Cu' = \gamma_kq_k' and X_k\cdot Au = \lambda_kq_k, with q_k = X_k\cdot u.
Part 3. In the state U = (u, u') the generator is B = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & I \\ -A & -C\end{smallmatrix}\right). In the basis (X_1, 0), (0, X_1), \dots, (X_n, 0), (0, X_n) it splits into 2\times2 blocks B_k = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -\lambda_k & -\gamma_k\end{smallmatrix}\right), with characteristic polynomial s^2 + \gamma_ks + \lambda_k. A 2\times2 matrix with two distinct eigenvalues has two independent eigenvectors. If the eigenvalue s_0 is repeated, B_k - s_0 is not zero (its top right entry is 1), so it has rank 1 and B_k has only one eigenvector: a Jordan block. B has a basis of eigenvectors exactly when every block does.
Light friction. For \gamma_k^2 < 4\lambda_k the roots are s = -\gamma_k/2 \pm i\sqrt{\lambda_k - \gamma_k^2/4}, and the real solutions are q_k = e^{-\gamma_kt/2}\big(a\cos\tilde\omega_kt + b\sin\tilde\omega_kt\big) with \tilde\omega_k = \sqrt{\lambda_k - \gamma_k^2/4}.
Why C must be symmetric. Friction that turns motion into heat comes from a dissipation function \tfrac12\,u'\cdot Cu', as Rayleigh introduced it, and is symmetric. An antisymmetric velocity term, such as a spinning object’s gyroscopic force, does no work and can commute with A (for A = \omega^2I it commutes with everything), yet its modes are rotating motions with complex shapes such as (1, \pm i), not real standing shapes.


Two piano strings in tune. Two strings tuned alike on one bridge, one mode each, have A = \omega_0^2I and, through the bridge they both drive, the friction C = r\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 1\\1 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\right): level 2, since a multiple of the identity commutes with every matrix. The shared eigenvectors are (1, 1), swinging together and fading at the rate r, and (1, -1), swinging oppositely, whose pushes on the bridge cancel, so the bridge does not drain it (only the strings’ own, smaller losses do). An unequal strike starts both, so each string’s motion decays in two stages, fast then slow.4
4 G. Weinreich, “Coupled piano strings”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 62 (1977), 1474–1484, and The coupled motion of piano strings, in Five Lectures on the Acoustics of the Piano, Royal Swedish Academy of Music, 1990, especially Two or more strings.


DetailsThe two-string model, and what it leaves to level 3

A piano note has two or three strings tuned alike on one bridge. Keep one mode per string, one number q_j each; in tune, A = \omega_0^2I on the pair. The bridge, driven by both strings at once, gives each a friction in proportion to its motion, C = r\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 1\\1 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\right), symmetric (the strings’ own losses aside). For (1, 1), \gamma = 2r: both push the yielding bridge, and the mode fades at the rate \gamma/2 = r; for (1, -1), \gamma = 0. An even hammer starts only (1, 1); an unequal strike starts both, in real modes, exactly in or out of step. This is the first half of Weinreich’s explanation (G. Weinreich, The coupled motion of piano strings, in Five Lectures on the Acoustics of the Piano, 1990): in this exact model the slow mode does not push the bridge at all, so it would hardly be heard; he showed that the strings’ slight mistuning, together with the hammer’s small irregularities, governs the aftersound, which is level 3.




Level 3 · The general case
The equation is any U' = BU. With a basis of eigenvectors it is modal, its modes in general complex: the entries of W have different phases, so parts of the shape peak at different moments.
The same two strings, mistuned. With A = \operatorname{diag}(\omega_1^2, \omega_2^2), \omega_1 \ne \omega_2, A no longer commutes with C. For a mistuning \delta = \omega_1 - \omega_2 about as large as r the modes are strongly complex: in each the strings swing out of step by an angle other than 0^\circ or 180^\circ, and both modes push the bridge, so the slow one is heard: the aftersound (numbers in the fold).
Radiation lands here too. Sound carried into unbounded air is a loss that depends on the shape and frequency, and the problem is no longer self-adjoint.



DetailsThe two strings, in tune and mistuned, in numbers uses complex numbers

This is a toy model: each string reduced to one mode, the bridge to the friction C = r\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right), and the strings’ own losses left out. For light friction and small mistuning, write u = \operatorname{Re}\big(a(t)\,e^{i\bar\omega t}\big) with \bar\omega = (\omega_1 + \omega_2)/2 and a slowly changing complex column a. Keeping first-order terms in r and \delta, the equation becomes 
a' = M a, \qquad M = \begin{pmatrix} i\delta/2 - r/2 & -r/2 \\ -r/2 & -i\delta/2 - r/2\end{pmatrix} ,
 with eigenvalues -\tfrac r2 \pm \tfrac12\sqrt{r^2 - \delta^2}.

In tune, \delta = 0: eigenvalues 0 and -r, eigenvectors (1, -1) and (1, 1), real.
Mistuned by less than r (at \delta = 0.6\,r: the strings swing equally far in each mode, 37^\circ apart in the nearly-together mode, fading at 0.9\,r, and 143^\circ apart in the nearly-opposite one, fading at 0.1\,r): both modes at one frequency, fading at the different rates \tfrac r2 \mp \tfrac12\sqrt{r^2 - \delta^2}. The eigenvector ratio a_2/a_1 = (i\delta/2 \mp \tfrac12\sqrt{r^2 - \delta^2})\cdot 2/r has modulus 1 and a phase other than 0 and 180^\circ. For \delta = 0.6\,r: rates 0.1\,r and 0.9\,r, ratios -0.8 + 0.6i and 0.8 + 0.6i, phases 143^\circ and 37^\circ.
Mistuned by exactly r: the two eigenvalues coincide at -r/2 with the single eigenvector (1, i), a Jordan block.
Mistuned by more than r: the frequencies split by \sqrt{\delta^2 - r^2} and both modes fade at the rate r/2: the strings beat.

A numerical check of the full equations u'' + Cu' + Au = 0, with r at 2% of \omega_0 and \delta = 0.6\,r, gives the same phases to within 0.01^\circ.

title: When does an equation have a spectrum?
text:
The deeper theory
This section needs linear algebra and analysis; the counterexamples and what you hear can be read without it.
Self-adjoint A \ge 0: the spectral theorem. On a Hilbert space of shapes (with an inner product, and limits), von Neumann’s spectral theorem5 represents A as multiplication by \lambda on its spectral parts, which defines \varphi(A): multiply the part at \lambda by \varphi(\lambda). This always expresses the solution through A’s spectrum, 
u(t) = \cos\!\big(t\sqrt{A}\big)\,f + \frac{\sin\!\big(t\sqrt{A}\big)}{\sqrt{A}}\,g ,
 for starting shape f and velocity g, reading \sin(t\sqrt A)/\sqrt A as t on drifts. For a matrix, \cos(t\sqrt A)f = \sum_i\cos(t\sqrt{\lambda_i})\,(X_i\cdot f)\,X_i: level 1’s formula. The spectrum is the set of numbers z for which A - z has no bounded inverse; for self-adjoint A \ge 0 it lies in [0, \infty).
5 J. von Neumann, “Allgemeine Eigenwerttheorie Hermitescher Funktionaloperatoren”, Mathematische Annalen 102 (1930), 49–131, and Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik, Springer, 1932; Wikipedia, Spectral theorem.A list of notes exactly when the resolvent is compact. The resolvent (A - z)^{-1} solves Au - zu = f for u. An operator is compact if it maps bounded sets to sets with compact closure; on a Hilbert space, equivalently, it is a limit in norm of operators with finite-dimensional range. For self-adjoint A \ge 0, (A + 1)^{-1} is compact exactly when the spectrum is a discrete list, eigenvalues \lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \cdots \to \infty of finite multiplicity, with eigenvectors forming an orthonormal basis (fold). Then the formula is a sum over modes, a list of notes, and with A > 0 the modes of B form an orthonormal basis of the energy space, the states (u, u') of finite energy. In finite dimensions every operator is compact; for continuous objects, this is what “the object is finite” means.
Which objects have it. Strings and tubes, by Sturm–Liouville theory;6 bars, by the same theorem through a compact Green’s operator; drums on a bounded region with a reasonable edge, by Rellich’s theorem7 (fold). Courant and Hilbert treat all of these.8 Which shapes share a list of notes: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
6 Wikipedia, Sturm–Liouville theory.7 F. Rellich, “Ein Satz über mittlere Konvergenz”, Nachrichten von der Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen, Mathematisch-Physikalische Klasse (1930), 30–35.8 R. Courant and D. Hilbert, Methods of Mathematical Physics, vol. 1, Interscience, 1953, chapters V and VI.The infinite string: spectral, but no list of notes. On the whole line A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 is self-adjoint and \ge 0 with spectrum [0, \infty) and no eigenvectors; the resolvent is not compact. The formula still holds, the sum over modes becoming the Fourier transform, 
u(x, t) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\Big(\hat f(k)\cos(ckt) + \hat g(k)\,\frac{\sin(ckt)}{ck}\Big)e^{ikx}\,dk ,
 a continuous spread of frequencies.
Without symmetry (friction, radiation), for losses that only remove energy, the motion still exists and is unique (a semigroup), but the eigenvectors may fail to form a basis, and whether they form a Riesz basis has to be proved case by case.9 For a string with friction varying along it they do,10 and decaying modes can still make the motion grow for a while.11 Details in the fold.
9 I. C. Gohberg and M. G. Krein, Introduction to the Theory of Linear Nonselfadjoint Operators, Translations of Mathematical Monographs 18, American Mathematical Society, 1969.10 S. Cox and E. Zuazua, “The rate at which energy decays in a damped string”, Communications in Partial Differential Equations 19 (1994), 213–243 (DOI).11 L. N. Trefethen and M. Embree, Spectra and Pseudospectra: The Behavior of Nonnormal Matrices and Operators, Princeton University Press, 2005.Nonlinear or time-dependent equations have no spectrum in this sense: by the criterion, their solutions are not all the combinations of a fixed set of modes.



PreciselyWhich objects have a compact resolvent, and solutions in the energy sense uses functional analysis


Strings and tubes: Sturm–Liouville theory. On a finite interval, -(pu')' + qu = \lambda\rho u with p, \rho > 0 and a condition at each end has simple eigenvalues \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 < \cdots \to \infty and eigenfunctions forming an orthogonal basis.
Bars: the same theorem through a compact Green’s operator. The fourth-order bar is not a classical Sturm–Liouville problem, but (A + 1)^{-1} is f \mapsto \int G(x, y)f(y)\,dy with a kernel G, the Green’s function, continuous on the square [0, L]^2, which makes it compact.
Drums: Rellich’s theorem (F. Rellich, “Ein Satz über mittlere Konvergenz”, 1930; Wikipedia, Rellich–Kondrachov theorem), on a bounded region with a reasonable edge: any set of shapes whose energies \iint(|\nabla u|^2 + u^2) are bounded by one number has compact closure in L^2, so the resolvent is compact. For a head fixed at its rim any bounded region will do; with a free edge, very irregular regions can fail.

Solutions in the energy sense. For a start of finite energy the formula gives the one motion of finite energy, which conserves it. A plucked string’s kink has no second derivative, so the plucked string solves u_{tt} = -Au in this sense, not point by point.





ProofA list of notes exactly when the resolvent is compact uses functional analysis

Let A \ge 0 be self-adjoint on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space H. Claim: R = (A + 1)^{-1} is compact if and only if H has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors X_k of A whose eigenvalues \lambda_k have finite multiplicity and tend to \infty.
If R is compact. R is bounded, with \|R\| \le 1 because \langle(A + 1)u, u\rangle \ge \|u\|^2; it is self-adjoint; and it is one-to-one, having the inverse A + 1. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators gives an orthonormal basis of the closure of its range, which is H because R is self-adjoint and one-to-one, made of eigenvectors RX_k = \mu_kX_k with \mu_k \to 0, each nonzero \mu_k of finite multiplicity, and no \mu_k = 0. Applying A + 1 gives X_k = \mu_k(A + 1)X_k, so AX_k = \lambda_kX_k with \lambda_k = 1/\mu_k - 1 \to \infty.
If such a basis exists. List the \lambda_k in increasing order. Then Rf = \sum_k(1 + \lambda_k)^{-1}\langle f, X_k\rangle X_k. Its truncations R_N, summing over k \le N, have finite-dimensional range, and \|R - R_N\| = \sup_{k > N}(1 + \lambda_k)^{-1} \to 0. A limit in norm of such operators is compact.
The energy space. Measure the energy of a state by \|(u, v)\|_E^2 = \langle Au, u\rangle + \langle v, v\rangle. For A > 0 with such a basis, the states W_{k,\pm} = (X_k, \pm i\omega_kX_k)/\sqrt{2\lambda_k}, \omega_k = \sqrt{\lambda_k}, have \|W_{k,\pm}\|_E^2 = (\lambda_k + \omega_k^2)/2\lambda_k = 1, are mutually perpendicular (for the pair, \lambda_k + (i\omega_k)\overline{(-i\omega_k)} = \lambda_k - \omega_k^2 = 0), and span the energy space; so they form an orthonormal basis of it, and the system is modal in the sense of Definition 3.





PreciselyWithout symmetry: semigroups, Riesz bases and growth before decay uses functional analysis

Semigroups. For a damped string or drum, energy can only decrease, \operatorname{Re}\langle BU, U\rangle_E \le 0 in the energy inner product, and B generates a contraction semigroup e^{tB}: bounded operators with e^{(t + t')B} = e^{tB}e^{t'B}, e^{0B} = I, continuous in t, sending the starting state to the state at time t, provided also that 1 - B is onto (together: B is maximally dissipative; the Lumer–Phillips theorem). This gives existence and uniqueness without any modes.
Riesz bases. In finite dimensions the only way to lack a basis of eigenvectors is a Jordan block. In infinite dimensions the eigenvectors can be complete (no state is perpendicular to all of them) and still not be a basis, or be a basis in which expansions are unstable. The property that makes mode expansions behave like orthonormal ones is a Riesz basis: the image of an orthonormal basis under a bounded operator with a bounded inverse; equivalently, every state is uniquely U = \sum_kc_kW_k with m\sum_k|c_k|^2 \le \|U\|^2 \le M\sum_k|c_k|^2 for fixed 0 < m \le M. I. C. Gohberg and M. G. Krein, Introduction to the Theory of Linear Nonselfadjoint Operators (Translations of Mathematical Monographs 18, American Mathematical Society, 1969), is the classical account of when the eigenvectors of a non-self-adjoint operator are complete or form a basis. For the string u_{tt} + 2a(x)\,u_t = u_{xx} on a finite interval, ends tied, with a friction coefficient a of bounded variation, S. Cox and E. Zuazua proved that the eigenvectors form a Riesz basis of the energy space, and that the energy decays at exactly the rate set by the slowest-fading mode (“The rate at which energy decays in a damped string”, Communications in Partial Differential Equations 19 (1994), 213–243, DOI).
Growth before decay. Even with a basis of decaying modes, a non-normal B, one that does not commute with its adjoint, so that its eigenvectors are not perpendicular, can make the size of the state grow for a while. The smallest example: B = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} -1 & 10 \\ 0 & -2\end{smallmatrix}\right) has modes fading at the rates 1 and 2, with the nearly parallel eigenvectors (1, 0) and (-10, 1). Starting from U(0) = (0, 1) = 10\,(1, 0) + (-10, 1), a near cancellation of two large modes, 
U(t) = \big(10\,(e^{-t} - e^{-2t}),\ e^{-2t}\big),
 which reaches size about 2.5 near t = 0.7 before it decays: the two modes fade at different rates and stop cancelling. Pseudospectra, the sets of z where \|(B - z)^{-1}\| is large, measure this (L. N. Trefethen and M. Embree, Spectra and Pseudospectra: The Behavior of Nonnormal Matrices and Operators, Princeton University Press, 2005).
Radiation. For an object radiating into unbounded air, the slowly fading “modes” are resonances: complex frequencies at which the resolvent, continued past the real axis, has poles. Expansions in them hold only in restricted senses.

title: When does an equation have a spectrum?
text:
Counterexamples, smallest first
1. A drift: x'' = 0. The generator B = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & 1\\0 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\right) has only the eigenvalue 0 and only the eigenvectors along (1, 0), so x = a + bt with b \ne 0 is not a combination of modes: a Jordan block. You hear nothing. In instruments: the two-bead ring, a free bar or drum sliding as a whole; split off.
2. Critical damping: u'' + 2u' + u = 0. The roots of s^2 + 2s + 1 = (s + 1)^2 coincide, B = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & 1\\-1 & -2\end{smallmatrix}\right) has the single eigenvector (1, -1), and the solutions are (a + bt)\,e^{-t}: the same Jordan block, moved by friction. You hear no ring: released, the mass creeps back to rest without swinging.
3. A property that changes in time. In Mathieu’s equation x'' = -(1 + \varepsilon\cos 2t)\,x the stiffness wobbles,12 and differentiating a solution adds the term 2\varepsilon\sin(2t)\,x: no modes e^{st}W. By Floquet’s theorem the solutions are combinations of e^{\mu t}p(t) with p periodic, and for every small \varepsilon \neq 0 one exponent has a positive real part, about \varepsilon/4: parametric resonance, as when a child pumps a swing.13 A slow change is gentler: a talking drum’s player squeezes its cords while it rings,14 and when the tension changes slowly compared with one swing, each mode keeps its shape and its frequency follows the tension, to a good approximation. You hear the pitch glide with the squeeze, even within one stroke.
12 Wikipedia, Mathieu function.13 G. Floquet, “Sur les équations différentielles linéaires à coefficients périodiques”, Annales scientifiques de l’École Normale Supérieure, 2e série, 12 (1883), 47–88.14 Wikipedia, Talking drum.15 Wikipedia, Pendulum (mechanics).16 J. O. Smith III, Tension modulation, in Physical Audio Signal Processing, CCRMA, Stanford; F. Avanzini, R. Marogna and B. Bank, “Efficient synthesis of tension modulation in strings and membranes based on energy estimation”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 131 (2012), 897–906; N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 5 (nonlinear systems) and chapter 18 (the kettledrum’s pitch drop).17 Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapter 20 (cymbals and gongs); the fold below gives the papers.4. A force not proportional to the displacement. The wide pendulum, x'' = -\sin x, is nonlinear and softening: wider swings are slower.15 Strings and drumheads stiffen instead, so a loud stroke starts sharp and its pitch drops as it fades.16 You hear pitch that moves with loudness: a hard guitar pluck’s twang, a gong’s glide; and a tamtam’s shimmer builds up as energy moves into higher modes.17



DetailsSoftening, stiffening, and what you hear uses no extra mathematics

The pendulum swung wide, x'' = -\sin x, is nonlinear (\sin 2x \neq 2\sin x, so twice a solution is not one) and softening: its force grows less than in proportion, so wider swings are slower; out to 90^\circ a swing takes 18% longer than a small one (Wikipedia, Pendulum (mechanics)). Strings and drumheads go the other way: a wide swing stretches them and raises the average tension, so a loud stroke starts sharp and its pitch drops as it fades. You hear a hard guitar pluck’s twang; the slight pitch drop of a loud kettledrum stroke; a gong’s pitch glide, up for some gongs and down for others, depending on the shell’s curvature and thickness (N. H. Fletcher, “Nonlinear frequency shifts in quasispherical-cap shells: Pitch glide in Chinese gongs”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 78 (1985), 2069–2073); and a tamtam’s or cymbal’s shimmer building up after the strike, as the nonlinearity passes energy from low modes into high ones (K. A. Legge and N. H. Fletcher, “Nonlinearity, chaos, and the sound of shallow gongs”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 86 (1989), 2439–2442). In a modal system each mode’s amount evolves on its own, so energy cannot flow between modes.


5. Rayleigh’s self-sustained oscillator. In Rayleigh’s equation,18 
x'' - \varepsilon\,\big(x' - \tfrac13 x'^3\big) + x = 0 ,
 the middle term feeds energy in when the motion is slow and takes it out when it is fast. Every motion except rest settles into one repeating cycle, a limit cycle,19 of amplitude about 2 and angular frequency 1 - \varepsilon^2/16 + \cdots, near the linear value 1. It has no modes; being periodic, its partials sit at exact whole-number multiples. You hear the steady tone of a bowed string, a reed or a player’s lips, exactly harmonic for as long as the player keeps going; and a harmonica’s bent notes, where the player’s mouth, with the hole’s other reed, pulls the playing frequency.20
18 Lord Rayleigh, “On maintained vibrations”, Philosophical Magazine, series 5, 15 (1883), 229–235.19 Wikipedia, Limit cycle.20 H. T. Bahnson, J. F. Antaki and Q. C. Beery, “Acoustical and physical dynamics of the diatonic harmonica”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 103 (1998), 2134–2144.6. The infinite string. On the whole line, u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx} is linear, unchanging in time, symmetric and positive, with no allowed eigenvectors: spectral (the deeper theory), no list of notes. You hear a click: a pluck splits into two half-height bumps that run apart, and each point falls still once they have passed.

The counterexamples, smallest first.







Counterexample
What fails
What you hear




1 drift
a full set of eigenvectors
nothing


2 critical damping
the same, with friction
no ring


3 pumped swing; talking drum
unchanging in time
growth; a gliding pitch


4 wide pendulum; loud strings, heads, gongs
linearity
pitch moving with loudness; shimmer


5 Rayleigh’s oscillator
linearity, with energy fed in
a steady, exactly harmonic tone


6 infinite string
finite size
a click






PreciselyThe counterexamples in equations uses differential equations

Stability. An unstable rest, x'' = +x (A = -1), is modal, with the real exponents s = \pm1, but one mode runs away exponentially: the opening statement’s “stable” is A \ge 0, and after any drifts (\lambda = 0) are split off, A > 0.
The pumped swing. For x'' + (1 + \varepsilon\cos 2t)x = 0 the map from the state at time 0 to the state at time \pi is a fixed matrix P (the coefficient has period \pi). Floquet’s theorem (G. Floquet, “Sur les équations différentielles linéaires à coefficients périodiques”, Annales scientifiques de l’École Normale Supérieure, 2e série, 12 (1883), 47–88) writes every solution, when P has two distinct eigenvalues as here, as a combination of e^{\mu t}p(t) with p of period \pi and e^{\mu\pi} an eigenvalue of P (\mu may be complex). A numerical computation of P gives the growth rate \operatorname{Re}\mu = 0.0125, 0.0250, 0.0499 for \varepsilon = 0.05, 0.1, 0.2: about \varepsilon/4.
The slow change. For x'' + \omega(t)^2x = 0 with \omega changing slowly compared with one swing, x \approx (a/\sqrt{\omega(t)})\cos\big(\int_0^t\omega\,dt' + \varphi\big): the frequency follows \omega(t), and the energy divided by the frequency stays nearly constant (an adiabatic invariant).
The wide pendulum. The period of x'' = -\sin x with amplitude x_0 is 4K(\sin^2(x_0/2)), where K(m) = \int_0^{\pi/2}(1 - m\sin^2\phi)^{-1/2}\,d\phi, against 2\pi for small swings; at x_0 = 90^\circ the ratio is 1.180.
Rayleigh’s oscillator. A numerical run of x'' - \varepsilon(x' - x'^3/3) + x = 0 settles to angular frequency 0.99938, 0.9944, 0.9847 for \varepsilon = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, against 1 - \varepsilon^2/16 = 0.99938, 0.99438, 0.98438, with amplitude about 2. By contrast, a linear system driven by a periodic force is solved by its modes, and without friction the response at an exact resonance grows in proportion to time.
Spinning objects. Gyroscopic forces Gu' with G antisymmetric do no work and need no friction, yet the equation is not of the form Mu'' = -Ku: the classical theory of small oscillations covers “natural” mechanical systems, whose energy is kinetic plus stored, without such terms.
The surrounding air. Treated as not squeezable near a drumhead, the air adds a fixed, symmetric, positive added mass, a generalized eigenvalue problem AX = \omega^2(1 + M_{\text{air}}/\sigma)X inside level 1 once lengths are measured with the masses as weights, \langle x, (\sigma + M_{\text{air}})y\rangle, as in the unequal-masses fold. Exactly, the added mass depends on the frequency and is complex, because sound radiates away into unbounded air, and the modes become resonances that fade at the rate the head radiates energy.
No edges. On the whole line, -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 has the continuous spectrum [0, \infty) and no eigenfunctions with finite \int|X|^2. With u_t(x, 0) = 0, d’Alembert’s solution u(x, t) = \tfrac12\big(f(x - ct) + f(x + ct)\big) shows the two half-height bumps; once both have passed a point, the string there is at rest.

title: When does an equation have a spectrum?
text:
Back to what you hear
The motion is not yet the sound. Between the object and your ear sit the instrument’s body (a violin’s box, a piano’s soundboard), the air and the room, and each is a linear filter that doesn’t change in time; for a room this holds very well at the pressures of music, as long as nothing in it moves.21 Such a filter keeps every f_k and \tau_k, changes the amounts a_k and phases \varphi_k, and adds its own ringing: the body’s resonances, and the room’s reverberation,22 which goes on after the instrument’s modes have faded and is how a room lengthens what you hear. The reason is the one in why modes exist: a filter that is the same at every moment sends e^{st} to a multiple of e^{st}, plus terms at its own exponents (fold). So the instrument’s part of the sound is 
p(t) = \sum_k a_k\,e^{-t/\tau_k}\cos(2\pi f_kt + \varphi_k) ,
 one term per mode, s = -1/\tau_k \pm 2\pi i f_k. The equation of motion (the operator, together with friction and radiation) fixes the f_k and \tau_k; the playing, the radiation and where you listen fix the a_k.
21 D. Masovic, Room Acoustics, lecture notes, TU Berlin, 2021.22 Wikipedia, Reverberation.


ProofA filter keeps every exponent and adds its own uses integrals

A linear filter that is the same at every moment, at rest before the input v starts at t = 0, has output p(t) = \int_0^t h(t - t')\,v(t')\,dt', where h is its response to a sudden tap. Take a body with finitely many decaying resonances, h(t) = \sum_jb_je^{r_jt} with \operatorname{Re} r_j < 0, and the input v(t) = e^{st} with s different from every r_j. Then 
p(t) = \sum_j b_je^{r_jt}\int_0^te^{(s - r_j)t'}\,dt' = H(s)\,e^{st} - \sum_j\frac{b_j}{s - r_j}\,e^{r_jt}, \qquad H(s) = \sum_j\frac{b_j}{s - r_j} .
 The input’s exponent s, and with it its frequency and fading time, comes out unchanged, multiplied by the number H(s): its size scaled by |H(s)| and its phase shifted by the angle of H(s). The other terms are the filter’s own ringing, at its own exponents r_j. By linearity a sum of modes passes term by term, and a real input, the sum of a mode and its conjugate, gives a real output. A propagation delay d multiplies e^{st} by e^{-sd}, again the same exponent.


The four aspects of sound, from the three lists. Post 1 defines pitch, loudness, timbre and duration as things we hear. What each is heard from, through the ear’s own weighting, is a fact about hearing, from psychoacoustics, not mathematics:23
23 B. C. J. Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, 6th ed., Emerald, Bingley, 2012 (reissued by Brill, Leiden, 2013), chapters 4, 6 and 8 (loudness, pitch, timbre); ISO 226:2023, Acoustics — Normal equal-loudness-level contours; S. S. Stevens, “On the psychophysical law”, Psychological Review 64 (1957), 153–181, and Wikipedia, Sone, for “twice as loud per 10 dB”.
The four aspects, and what each is heard from.







Aspect
Heard from
Set by




Pitch
mainly where the f_k sit: for a single tone whose prominent partials lie near a harmonic series in the pitch range, that series’ base
the equation of motion


Loudness
the sizes a_k, weighted by frequency (equal-loudness contours); about twice as loud per 10 dB
the playing, the radiation, where you listen


Timbre
all three lists, f_k, a_k and \tau_k, especially early on, plus noise that is not a mode
all of these


Duration
the fading times \tau_k, and when the player stops or damps the note
friction and radiation, and the player



The four routes to a clear pitch, now explained. Post 1 lists four ways to partials at or very near whole-number multiples of one frequency. Each is a statement about these lists.

By nature: strings and air columns. On an interval with tied or open ends, -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 gives f_n = nc/2L, for the two reasons given for the loop of string; a tube closed at one end, like a clarinet’s, gives the odd multiples (2n - 1)c/4L.
By design. Added stiffness never lowers an eigenvalue and added mass never raises one (the min–max principle), so makers reshape the operator until the modes that matter land near the lines: a kettledrum’s air loading,24 a marimba bar’s undercut,25 the tabla’s loaded patch,26 a bell’s profile (most principal partials on a harmonic series; the tierce, a minor third above the prime, is not on the series).27
By suppression. A short \tau_k, like a kalimba tine’s fast-dying off-line overtone,28 or a small a_k and short \tau_k together, like a kettledrum’s off-line round modes, which the usual playing spot starts more weakly than the spoke modes (the drums in post 3) and which radiate their energy away fast.29
By a periodic drive: bow and breath. Rayleigh’s oscillator, counterexample 5: a limit cycle, exactly periodic and so exactly harmonic; the resonator’s modes shape which partials are strong.

24 R. S. Christian, R. E. Davis, A. Tubis, C. A. Anderson, R. I. Mills and T. D. Rossing, “Effects of air loading on timpani membrane vibrations”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 76 (1984), 1336–1345.25 Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapter 19 (mallet percussion: the marimba’s undercut).26 C. V. Raman, “The Indian musical drums”, Proceedings of the Indian Academy of Sciences A 1 (1934), 179–188.27 Wikipedia, Strike tone.28 D. M. F. Chapman, The sound of the African thumb piano (kalimba), Acoustics’08 Paris, 2008.29 Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapter 18 (drums: the strike point and radiation); T. A. Packer, Acoustics of the Orchestral Kettledrum, master’s thesis, University of Durham, 1993.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← Kalimba · Piano → · Glossary
Nowhere: a blown reed never sounds them. Blown, the reed swings in one repeating cycle and chops the air into identical puffs, and a sound that repeats has partials only at whole-number multiples of its rate, so 6.27× and 17.55× have nowhere to appear. Pluck the reed, then blow it, and compare the stems with the gray whole-number lines.
The reason, in one sentence: where a blown note’s partials sit is decided by the fact that the motion repeats, not by the reed’s own frequencies.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
The reed’s equation
A reed is a thin brass bar riveted at one end over a slot and free at the other: the kalimba tine’s bar, so it has the tine’s equation (derived in the fold below). With u(x, t) the reed’s sideways displacement at distance x from the rivet, 
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -Au, \qquad Au = \kappa^2u_{xxxx}, \\
\kappa^2 = \frac{EI}{\rho S} = \frac{Eh^2}{12\rho} .
\end{gathered}
 In words: brass resists bending, and the force per unit mass pulling each point back is the shape’s fourth derivative times a constant set by the brass and the thickness.1 Here E is brass’s Young’s modulus, \rho its density, S the area of the reed’s cross-section and I its second moment of area; the last form is for a rectangular reed of width w and thickness h, where I = wh^3/12 and S = wh. The ends complete the operator: at the rivet the reed can neither move nor tilt, u = u_x = 0; at the free tip nothing bends or pushes it, u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0.
1 N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 2 (transverse vibrations of a bar); Wikipedia, Free reed aerophone.


DetailsWhere the equation comes from partial derivatives, an integral over a cross-section

Bend the reed, and fibers on the outside of the curve stretch while those on the inside compress; a middle line, the neutral axis, keeps its length. For small slopes the curvature is u_{xx}, and a fiber at height y above the neutral axis is stretched by the fraction -y\,u_{xx}, so by Hooke’s law it carries the force per unit area -E\,y\,u_{xx}. Over the cross-section these forces cancel, but their turning effects add up to the bending moment 
\begin{gathered}
M = \int y\,(E\,y\,u_{xx})\,dA = EI\,u_{xx}, \\
I = \int y^2\,dA .
\end{gathered}
 Each face of a thin slice also carries a sideways shear force V. A thin slice’s rotational inertia is negligible, so the turning effects on it balance: V\,dx + dM = 0, that is, V = -M_x = -EI\,u_{xxx}. The shear forces on the two faces differ by V_x\,dx, which by Newton’s law accelerates the slice’s mass \rho S\,dx: 
\rho S\,u_{tt} = V_x = -EI\,u_{xxxx},
 the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation, with \kappa^2 = EI/\rho S. A fourth-order equation needs two conditions at each end. The riveted end can neither move nor tilt: u = u_x = 0. At the free tip nothing bends or pushes the reed: M = 0 and V = 0, that is, u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0. For a rectangular reed, I = wh^3/12 and S = wh, so \kappa^2 = Eh^2/12\rho.
The model assumes small motions, a uniform bar clamped at exactly one point, no damping and no air around the reed; it ignores the slices’ rotational inertia and shear deformation, which matter only for thick bars and high modes (Wikipedia, Euler–Bernoulli beam theory). Real reeds are not exactly uniform, so their overtones differ somewhat from the ideal values below.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
Its spectrum: off the lines
The operator and the ends are the tine’s, so the spectrum is too. Writing \lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4, a shape that A only stretches exists exactly when 
\begin{gathered}
\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1, \\
\beta_nL = 1.8751,\ 4.6941,\ 7.8548, \dots,
\end{gathered}
 so the frequencies f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi = \kappa\beta_n^2/2\pi stand in the ratios 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : \cdots, off the whole-number lines.2 The fold below solves the equation step by step. The lowest is 
f_1 = \frac{(1.8751)^2}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{h}{L^2}\sqrt{\frac{E}{12\rho}} .
 The width w cancels: it decides how much air the reed moves, not its pitch. Low reeds are long, high reeds short.
2 Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 2: the clamped–free bar’s frequencies in the ratios 1 : 6.27 : 17.55.


PreciselyThe spectrum, step by step a 2×2 determinant

With \lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4 the mode equation AX = \lambda X is X'''' = \beta^4X, solved by \cos\beta x, \sin\beta x, \cosh\beta x and \sinh\beta x, where \cosh y = (e^y + e^{-y})/2 and \sinh y = (e^y - e^{-y})/2 are the hyperbolic functions. The rivet, X(0) = X'(0) = 0, leaves 
\begin{aligned}
X = {} & a\,(\cos\beta x - \cosh\beta x) \\
& + b\,(\sin\beta x - \sinh\beta x).
\end{aligned}
 With c_1 = \cos\beta L, s_1 = \sin\beta L, c_2 = \cosh\beta L, s_2 = \sinh\beta L, the free tip’s X''(L) = X'''(L) = 0 reads -(c_1 + c_2)a - (s_1 + s_2)b = 0 and (s_1 - s_2)a - (c_1 + c_2)b = 0. A solution other than a = b = 0 exists exactly when the determinant vanishes: 
\begin{aligned}
& (c_1 + c_2)^2 + (s_1 + s_2)(s_1 - s_2) \\
& \quad = 2 + 2c_1c_2 = 0,
\end{aligned}
 using c_1^2 + s_1^2 = 1 and c_2^2 - s_2^2 = 1. So \cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1. Since \cosh\beta L grows fast, \cos\beta L must be near 0, so \beta_nL is near (n - \tfrac12)\pi; numerically 1.8751, 4.6941, 7.8548, 10.9955. The ratios follow from f_n \propto \beta_n^2: (4.6941/1.8751)^2 \approx 6.27 and (7.8548/1.8751)^2 \approx 17.55. Pinned ends would give the sines and the ratios 1 : 4 : 9; the rivet and the free tip shift the first root most, which puts the ratios off the lines. Substituting \kappa = h\sqrt{E/12\rho} into f_1 = \kappa\beta_1^2/2\pi gives the formula for f_1 below.


Below, the plucked reed’s stems sit at this spectrum, off the lines; the blown reed’s sit on every line, with none at 6.27\times. Same reed, same operator; only the way it is played differs.


  
  
  Plucked (top): 1× and 6.27×, off the lines (17.55× is off the right edge). Blown (bottom): every stem on a line, none at 6.27×.


Plucked, the reed rings like a tine: it moves as \sum_n a_n e^{-t/\tau_n} X_n(x) \cos(2\pi f_n t), a sum of its modes, each fading at its own rate, so you hear the off-line overtones until they die. The demo’s plucked sound is made exactly this way, with illustrative fading times.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
Blown: one repeating cycle
Blown, the reed swings through its slot, opening and closing the air path hundreds of times a second. It becomes a valve, and the sound comes mainly from the chopped airflow, not from the reed’s own motion.3 A steadily blown reed settles into a motion that repeats exactly, at a playing frequency f_p slightly below its first mode’s frequency, so the puffs repeat at that rate too.4 So the reed’s first mode sets the pitch.
3 C. Pykett, The physics of free reeds, 2023: “it is the energy in the resulting repetitive puffs of air which produces the sounds we hear”.4 J. Cottingham, Acoustics of free-reed instruments, Physics Today 64(3), 2011, 44–48 (doi:10.1063/1.3563819), p. 45: “the sounding frequency of the blown reed is somewhat below the natural vibrating frequency of the reed tongue”, for the kind of reed that sounds in ordinary blowing and drawing.That the reed locks into one repeating motion is observed, not derived here (fold below). Granting it, the rest is mathematics:

The airflow repeats. Let q(t) be the airflow through the slot. In the steady oscillation it repeats every P = 1/f_p seconds: q(t + P) = q(t).
A repeating signal has only whole-number multiples. Any reasonable function of period P is a sum of \cos(2\pi nt/P) and \sin(2\pi nt/P) for n = 0, 1, 2, \dots, its Fourier series, so it contains only the frequencies nf_p.
So the note lands on the lines. The blown sound has frequencies only at whole-number multiples of the playing frequency, odd and even both strong.5 How strong each is depends on the shape of a single puff: short, sharp puffs give strong high partials.

5 C. Pykett, The physics of free reeds, 2023: “Both odd and even harmonics were strongly represented in the sounds of these reeds.”The argument uses only that the motion repeats, not which modes make it up. That is where the reed’s own overtones went.



DetailsWhy the reed locks into one repeating motion, and how the demo makes its sound

A steady oscillation kept going by a steady push is a self-sustained oscillation, and the repeating cycle it settles into a limit cycle; the bowed string and the clarinet reed are others, and the appendix gives the smallest example. That the blown reed settles into one is observed, and reproduced by nonlinear models of reeds; it is not derived here. A plausible picture, not a derivation: the airflow feeds energy mainly into the first mode, the other modes are not kept going at their own frequencies, and in the repeating cycle they move only as they are pushed, at whole-number multiples of f_p.
The demos’ blown sounds are models. The “Blow the C5 reed” and filing demos play one puff shape, chosen so that the open part of each cycle is short, repeated at the playing frequency: its whole-number multiples weaker overall as they go up. The chromatic harmonica further down passes the same puff train through two broad peaks, a stand-in for resonances of the player’s mouth and the instrument, and adds a little band-passed breath noise. The peaks were set by ear, not measured, so the timbre is approximate. The pitch and the whole-number spacing are not approximations.


The bowed string and the clarinet work the same way, but their own frequencies already sit on or near the lines, which hides the drive’s work. A free reed’s overtones are far off the lines, so here you can hear it.

section: Tuning a reed with a file
text:
Tuning a reed with a file
Reeds are tuned by scraping metal off the tongue: scraping near the tip raises the pitch, and scraping near the rivet lowers it.6 The first mode explains the direction: it bends most near the rivet and moves most near the tip. Thin the reed near the rivet and you remove stiffness where it counts, so the pitch drops; thin it near the tip and you remove mass where it counts, so the pitch rises. The Rayleigh quotient says this exactly: 
\omega_1^2 = \min_{u} \frac{\int_0^L EI\,(u'')^2\,dx}{\int_0^L \rho S\,u^2\,dx},
 the minimum over shapes u \ne 0 that satisfy the conditions at the rivet, attained by the first mode. It is a mass on a spring, \omega^2 = s/m, again: stiffness on top, weighted by where the reed bends, and mass at the bottom, weighted by where it moves. Try it below.
6 C. Pykett, The physics of free reeds, 2023, section “Tuning and voicing”: “Reeds are tuned by removing metal from the tongue. Removing it from the tip raises the pitch, and scraping it from nearer the riveted end lowers it.”

    Where to filebase
    
    Blow the filed reedBlow the original
    Filing removes a quarter of the thickness over about a tenth of the reed. The pitch change is estimated as in the fold below.
  




ProofWhy filing moves the pitch: stiffness against mass integration by parts, first-order approximation


The quotient. Multiply \rho S\,\omega^2X = (EI\,X'')'' by X and integrate by parts twice; the boundary terms vanish at the rivet and at the free tip. This gives \omega^2 = \int EI(X'')^2 / \int \rho S X^2 for every mode. That the first mode minimizes the quotient is the Rayleigh–Ritz principle (Wikipedia, Rayleigh quotient).
Small change. File the reed so that its thickness changes by \delta h(x) < 0. Then I \propto h^3 changes by \delta(EI) = 3EI\,\delta h/h, and S \propto h by \delta(\rho S) = \rho S\,\delta h/h, to first order, that is, ignoring terms in (\delta h)^2.
First order. Because the first mode minimizes the quotient, changing the shape slightly changes the quotient only by an amount proportional to the square of the change. So to first order one may keep the old mode shape X and change only the coefficients: 
\begin{gathered}
\delta(\omega^2) = \frac{\int \frac{\delta h}{h}\,B\,dx}{\int \rho S\,X^2\,dx}, \\
B = 3EI\,(X'')^2 - \omega^2\rho S\,X^2 .
\end{gathered}

Sign. Near the rivet X \approx 0 and X'' is largest, so B > 0 and, with \delta h < 0, \omega drops. Near the tip X'' = 0 and X is largest, so B < 0 and \omega rises. In between there is a point where filing changes nothing, to first order.

The demo uses the full quotient with the original mode shape, which is accurate to first order in the depth of filing.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
section: The player, and the chromatic slide
text:
The player, and the chromatic slide
The breath sets how hard the air flows. The reed’s frequency hardly varies with the wind pressure, which changes its loudness and the shape of each puff, and so the tone.7 A free reed loses little energy per cycle, so it is slow to start,8 and the note lasts as long as the breath. Skilled players bend some notes on a diatonic harmonica downward by coupling the reeds to resonances of their own mouth and throat: a case where the player does move the pitch.9 Both of the hole’s reeds, the blow reed and the draw reed over the same chamber, take part, and the bent note lies between their two notes.10
7 C. Pykett, The physics of free reeds, 2023: “its frequency hardly varies with variations in wind pressure which affect its loudness”; the pulse shape, and so the tone, changes with the pressure.8 C. Pykett, The physics of free reeds, 2023: “Another implication of its high Q is that the free reed comes onto speech relatively slowly.”9 J. Cottingham, Acoustics of free-reed instruments, Physics Today 64(3), 2011, 44–48: pitch bending through the player’s vocal tract.10 H. T. Bahnson, J. F. Antaki and Q. C. Beery, “Acoustical and physical dynamics of the diatonic harmonica”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 103 (1998), 2134–2144: in a bend the blow and draw reeds of the hole both vibrate, and the bent pitch lies between their natural frequencies.11 Wikipedia, Chromatic harmonica: a “sliding bar to redirect air” to a second reed plate, giving “the same scale a semitone higher in each hole”; solo tuning, blow C, E, G, C and draw D, F, A, B.A chromatic harmonica has two sets of reeds, the second tuned a semitone higher; in each set, every hole has a blow reed, sounded by breathing out, and a draw reed, sounded by breathing in. Pushing the slide moves a bar that sends the air to the other set, so every note rises a semitone. In solo tuning, the usual layout, each group of four holes holds C, E, G, C on the blow and D, F, A, B on the draw.11 Here is a whole one to play.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← Clarinet · Harmonica → · Glossary
A kalimba sounds clean because its off-line overtone dies within a fraction of a second, and the fundamental rings on alone. Tap a tine; then tick the box, which keeps the overtones ringing, and tap it again.
The reason, in one sentence: a tine springs back by resisting bending, which puts its overtones far off the whole-number lines, and the strongest of them starts loud but fades almost at once. The first half follows from Newton’s law; the second is measured.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
Where the equation comes from
A tine is under no tension: it springs back because steel resists being bent. Let u(x, t) be its height at distance x from the clamp. Bend it, and the steel on the outside of the curve stretches while the inside compresses; together these forces turn each cross-section, a bending moment M = EI\,u_{xx} proportional to the curvature (E is steel’s Young’s modulus, how stiff the material is, and I the second moment of area, how strongly the cross-section’s shape resists bending).
A thin slice of the tine cannot spin, so the moments on its two faces are balanced by a sideways shear force V = -M_x, and the difference of the shear forces on its two faces accelerates it. For a slice of density \rho and cross-sectional area S, Newton’s law gives 
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2 u_{xxxx}, \qquad \kappa^2 = \frac{EI}{\rho S},
 the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation, with four derivatives where the string had two.2
2 Wikipedia, Euler–Bernoulli beam theory; N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 2 (bars).3 Wikipedia, Cantilever: a beam supported at one end only.The ends complete the problem. The base is clamped: it can neither move nor tilt, u = u_x = 0. The tip is free: no moment and no shear force act there, u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0. A bar held like this is a cantilever.3 So the equation reads u_{tt} = -Au with 
A = \kappa^2\,\frac{d^4}{dx^4},
 acting on shapes with u = u_x = 0 at the clamp and u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 at the tip. The model assumes small slopes, a uniform bar clamped at exactly one point, and no friction.



DetailsThe slice, step by step an integral over a cross-section

Bend the bar, and a middle line, the neutral axis, keeps its length. For small slopes the curvature is u_{xx}, and a fiber at height y above the neutral axis is stretched by the fraction -y\,u_{xx}, so by Hooke’s law it carries the force per unit area -E\,y\,u_{xx}. Over the cross-section these forces cancel, but their turning effects add up to 
\begin{gathered}
M = -\int y(-Ey\,u_{xx})\,dA = EI\,u_{xx}, \\
I = \int y^2\,dA .
\end{gathered}
 A thin slice’s rotational inertia is negligible, so the turning effects on it balance: V\,dx + dM = 0, that is, V = -M_x = -EI\,u_{xxx}. The shear forces on the two faces differ by V_x\,dx, which accelerates the slice’s mass \rho S\,dx: \rho S\,u_{tt} = V_x = -EI\,u_{xxxx}. A fourth-order equation needs two conditions at each end, which the clamp and the free tip supply. The model ignores the slices’ rotational inertia and shear deformation, which matter only for thick bars and high modes (Wikipedia, Euler–Bernoulli beam theory).


What four derivatives do. Squeeze a shape into half the length and every rate of change along it doubles. A string’s pull depends on two derivatives, so it grows 2 \times 2 = 4 times; a tine’s push depends on four, so it grows 2^4 = 16 times. Short wiggles are far stiffer in a tine than in a string, and both of the tine’s surprises below come from this.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
The tine’s shapes
As for the string, the shapes that matter are the ones A only stretches, AX = \lambda X. Write \lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4, so that X'''' = \beta^4X. Four functions return to themselves after four derivatives: \cos\beta x and \sin\beta x, and \cosh\beta x and \sinh\beta x, the hyperbolic functions \cosh y = (e^y + e^{-y})/2 and \sinh y = (e^y - e^{-y})/2. The four end conditions are four equations for the four coefficients, and they have a solution other than zero exactly when 
\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1 .
 Since \cosh\beta L grows fast, \cos\beta L must be close to 0, so \beta L sits near (n - \tfrac12)\pi. Solved numerically, the roots are \beta_nL = 1.8751,\ 4.6941,\ 7.8548,\ 10.9955, \dots, and so 
\lambda_n = \kappa^2\beta_n^4, \qquad f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{\kappa\,\beta_n^2}{2\pi},
 in the ratios 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : 34.39, growing like (2n - 1)^2: off the whole-number lines.4 The first root is the furthest from its estimate, \pi/2 \approx 1.571, and that shift is what breaks the pattern: if every root sat exactly at (n - \tfrac12)\pi, the ratios would be the whole numbers 1 : 9 : 25.
4 N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 2: the clamped–free bar’s frequencies, in the ratios 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : 34.39.


DetailsThe mode condition from the four end conditions a 2×2 determinant

The clamp, X(0) = X'(0) = 0, leaves two constants: 
\begin{aligned}
X = {} & a\,(\cos\beta x - \cosh\beta x) \\
& + b\,(\sin\beta x - \sinh\beta x) .
\end{aligned}
 With the shorthand c_1 = \cos\beta L, s_1 = \sin\beta L, c_2 = \cosh\beta L, s_2 = \sinh\beta L, and dropping the common factors \beta^2 and \beta^3, the free tip’s X''(L) = 0 and X'''(L) = 0 read 
\begin{gathered}
-(c_1 + c_2)\,a - (s_1 + s_2)\,b = 0, \\
(s_1 - s_2)\,a - (c_1 + c_2)\,b = 0 .
\end{gathered}
 Two equations pa + qb = 0 and ra + sb = 0 have a solution other than a = b = 0 exactly when the determinant ps - qr vanishes. Here 
\begin{aligned}
& (c_1 + c_2)^2 + (s_1 + s_2)(s_1 - s_2) \\
& \quad = c_1^2 + s_1^2 + 2c_1c_2 + c_2^2 - s_2^2 \\
& \quad = 2 + 2c_1c_2 ,
\end{aligned}
 by c_1^2 + s_1^2 = 1 and c_2^2 - s_2^2 = 1. So a mode exists exactly when \cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1. The modes are X_n = \cosh\beta_n x - \cos\beta_n x - \sigma_n(\sinh\beta_n x - \sin\beta_n x), with \sigma_n = (\sinh\beta_nL - \sin\beta_nL)/(\cosh\beta_nL + \cos\beta_nL) from the second equation.





Reader questionWould other ends give whole numbers?

Yes, for some. A bar held in place at both ends but free to pivot has u = u_{xx} = 0 at each end. Then \sin(n\pi x/L) satisfies all four conditions, four derivatives multiply it by (n\pi/L)^4, and the frequency ratios are 1 : 4 : 9 : 16, whole numbers. The clamp and the free tip are what move the roots, and the first root most.


In the panel, each stem is one f_n on the pitch ruler of post 1, against its gray whole-number lines; 17.55× and 34.39× are off the right edge. A stem’s height is how hard that mode pushes on the bridge just after a pluck, the subject of the next section. Tap a stem to see its shape.


    Modes of one tine · tap a stem

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
The pluck: a click
Released at rest from the bent shape a thumb holds it in, the tine moves as a sum of its shapes, each swinging at its own frequency: 
u(x, t) = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} a_n \cos(2\pi f_n t)\,X_n(x) .
 In how far the tine swings, the first overtone is tiny: a_2 is 2.5% of a_1, because each mode gives way to the thumb in inverse proportion to its stiffness \lambda_n. But the kalimba’s body feels the push of the tine on the bridge, not its swing, and in that push the higher modes weigh more. There the first overtone starts at about 55% of the fundamental. That strong start is the click at the beginning of each note.



DetailsHow strongly a pluck at the tip starts each mode integration by parts


The pluck shape. Before release, a push F at the tip holds the tine still. Inside, nothing pushes, so EI\,u_0'''' = 0 and u_0 is a cubic. The clamp, the moment-free tip and the tip height h leave u_0 = h\,x^2(3L - x)/2L^3, with u_0'''(L) = -3h/L^3 \ne 0: the shear force F = 3EIh/L^3 of the thumb. The start is smooth, as it must be: a shape with a corner has u_x jumping, so u_{xx} contains a spike and the bending energy \tfrac12 EI\int (u_{xx})^2 is infinite, which a finite push cannot store. The start fails the tip condition u_{xxx}(L) = 0, but only where the thumb pushed. That is allowed: in post 2’s weak sense of solution, a solution is tested only against smooth shapes \varphi that satisfy all four end conditions, through \langle u(t), \varphi\rangle, so the series needs only a start of finite bending energy with u_0 = u_0' = 0 at the clamp; the tip’s conditions need not hold.
Split it into modes. Write u_0 = \sum_n a_n X_n, each mode scaled so that \int_0^L X_n^2\,dx = L, and compute \int_0^L EI\,u_0\,X_n''''\,dx in two ways. By the mode equation EI\,X_n'''' = \rho S\,\omega_n^2X_n, with \omega_n = 2\pi f_n, and because different modes are perpendicular, it equals \rho SL\,\omega_n^2\,a_n. Integrating by parts four times instead, every term vanishes except the tip’s shear force times X_n(L). So \rho SL\,\omega_n^2\,a_n = F\,X_n(L): mode n is a spring of stiffness proportional to \omega_n^2, pushed with a force proportional to its value at the tip.
Tip values. In the form of the fold above, \sigma_1 \approx 0.734, \sigma_2 \approx 1.018, and every mode has X_n(L) = \pm2 (a known property of clamped–free modes, easily confirmed numerically). So a_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2, and a_2/a_1 = 1/6.27^2 \approx 2.5\%.
Forces on the bridge. In this model the tine is clamped right at the bridge, so the forces at the clamp are the forces on the bridge. With X_n''(0) = 2\beta_n^2 and X_n'''(0) = -2\sigma_n\beta_n^3, and a_n \propto 1/\beta_n^4, the second mode’s bending moment at the clamp is (\beta_1/\beta_2)^2 \approx 16\% of the first’s, and its shear force (\sigma_2/\sigma_1)(\beta_1/\beta_2) \approx 1.39 \times 0.40 \approx 55\%. These are two measures of the push, not a range of uncertainty; the demo uses the shear force.

A real tine is held a little behind the bridge and rests on it partway along, rather than being clamped at one point. Chapman found that the measured overtone ratios are “correlated with the subdivided lengths of the vibrating beam”, which is one reason they spread around the ideal 6.27 (D. M. F. Chapman, The sound of the African thumb piano (kalimba), Acoustics’08 Paris, 2008).

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
Fading: the overtone goes first
The click is gone within a fraction of a second, while the fundamental rings on. This part is observed, not derived: the model has no friction, so in it every mode rings forever. The acoustician D. M. F. Chapman measured a Hugh Tracey kalimba and found one dominant overtone at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, near the ideal 6.27, and found that the off-line overtones die away rapidly.5
5 D. M. F. Chapman, The sound of the African thumb piano (kalimba), Acoustics’08 Paris, paper 5aMUf1, Acoustical Society of America, 2008: measured on “the Hugh Tracey Pentatonic Kalimba”; “a single overtone (f1) whose frequency ratio f1/f0 is about 5.9-6.8”; “the anharmonic overtones die away rapidly”.The demo’s sound is made this way. It adds the first five modes at the frequencies above, each starting with its strength in the push on the bridge; the fundamental fades over a couple of seconds and the overtones within a small fraction of that. Those fading times are illustrative, chosen to match Chapman’s observation. Tick the box and every mode fades as slowly as the fundamental: the same spectrum then clangs like a bell.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
What you hear
A click, then a clean note. What remains after the click is the fundamental alone, a single partial, and a single partial has a clear pitch at its own frequency. The spectrum alone would clang, as a bell’s does; the fading decides. The player sets the loudness by how far the tip is pushed, since every a_n grows in proportion to it.
Half the length, two octaves up. The numbers \beta_nL do not depend on the length, so f_n = \kappa\,(\beta_nL)^2/(2\pi L^2): a tine’s frequency goes as one over its length squared. Half the length gives four times the frequency, two octaves, where a string rises only one. That is why, in the demo, the low tines are not twice as long as the tines an octave above them. It is also why a small change of length goes a long way when a tine is tuned: its length is measured from where it is held down on the bridge, and longer is lower, shorter higher.6
6 Kalimba Magic, on tuning tines: “Making tines longer (from the point where they are held down on the bridge) will lower their pitch, and making them shorter will make their pitch higher.”
