title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← Violin · Kalimba → · Glossary
The ends. A flute is open at both ends and a clarinet is closed at the reed, and a tube closed at one end fits a quarter of a wave where an open tube fits a half, so the same length sounds an octave lower and has modes only at the odd multiples of its lowest frequency. Hold the blow button on the clarinet, then switch the same tube to a flute and blow again; the register key (on the flute it stands in for a faster, narrower airstream) makes either tube jump to its next mode.
The reason, in one sentence: the two tubes have the same operator with different ends, and the ends decide which shapes, and so which frequencies, the air can have.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
The tube’s equation
Let p(x, t) be the air pressure in the tube minus room pressure, at distance x from the reed end. Newton’s law on a thin slab of air, pushed by the pressure difference across it, together with the way air pushes back when squeezed, gives the wave equation again, the string’s equation, now for the pressure (the flute’s entry derives it): 
\begin{gathered}
p_{tt} = -Ap, \qquad Ap = -c^2p_{xx}, \\
c^2 = \frac{K}{\rho} .
\end{gathered}
 In words: the pressure at each point changes in proportion to how sharply the pressure shape bends. Here K is the air’s bulk modulus, its resistance to being squeezed, \rho its density, and c the speed of sound, about 343 m/s at 20 °C.1
1 Wikipedia, Speed of sound: about 343 m/s in dry air at 20 °C.Only the ends differ between a flute and a clarinet, and they are part of the operator A:

An open end meets the room, so the pressure there is room pressure, p = 0, a Dirichlet condition.2 The flute has two: p(0) = p(L) = 0.
The clarinet’s reed is nearly shut, so the air there cannot move back and forth, and air that never moves feels no net push: the pressure has no slope, p_x(0) = 0, a Neumann condition. Its bell is open, p(L) = 0.

2 J. Wolfe, Pipes and harmonics, UNSW: at an open end the “sound pressure (difference from atmospheric) is close to zero”.


DetailsThe reed end, the end correction, and what the model leaves out

Let \xi(x, t) be how far the air that normally sits at x has moved along the tube. Newton’s law on a slab is \rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x. At the reed the air cannot move, so \xi = 0 there at all times, so \xi_{tt} = 0, and Newton’s law gives p_x = 0. The air just outside an open end moves with the air inside, so the tube acts slightly longer, by about 0.6 of its radius, an amount called the end correction (J. Wolfe, Pipes and harmonics, UNSW: “usually about 0.6 times the radius”). The model assumes a narrow cylindrical tube, small pressure changes and no friction at the walls. A real clarinet’s bore is not exactly cylindrical, and its holes and bell matter; they refine the numbers below, not the picture (N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapters 8 and 15).

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
Two tubes, two spectra
The shapes the operator only stretches, AX_n = \lambda_nX_n, swing at f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi. With the flute’s ends they are the string’s sines; with the clarinet’s they are cosines that fit an odd number of quarter waves: 
\begin{aligned}
&\text{flute:} && X_n = \sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}, \\
& && f_n = n\,\frac{c}{2L}, \\
&\text{clarinet:} && X_n = \cos\frac{(2n - 1)\pi x}{2L}, \\
& && f_n = (2n - 1)\,\frac{c}{4L} .
\end{aligned}
 The flute’s modes sit at 1, 2, 3, 4, … times its lowest frequency, the clarinet’s at 1, 3, 5, 7, … times its lowest, and the clarinet’s lowest, c/4L, is half the flute’s c/2L.3
3 J. Wolfe, Pipes and harmonics, UNSW: closed cylindrical bores “have only odd harmonics starting one octave lower”.


PreciselyThe two spectra, step by step derivatives

Writing \lambda = c^2k^2, the mode equation -c^2X'' = \lambda X becomes X'' = -k^2X, solved by X = a\cos kx + b\sin kx, with f = \sqrt\lambda/2\pi = ck/2\pi.
Flute. X(0) = 0 forces a = 0, and X(L) = 0 needs \sin kL = 0, so kL = n\pi: one half wave, two half waves, and so on. So \lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2 and f_n = nc/2L.
Clarinet. X'(0) = bk = 0 forces b = 0, leaving X = \cos kx, and X(L) = 0 needs \cos kL = 0, so kL = (2n - 1)\pi/2: one quarter wave, three quarter waves, and so on. So \lambda_n = \big((2n - 1)\pi c/2L\big)^2 and f_n = (2n - 1)c/4L.
As for the string, integration by parts rules out \lambda \le 0, and every pressure shape is a sum of these modes; the appendix says when such a sum is guaranteed.




  
  
  The tubes' modes, as multiples of each tube's lowest frequency: open at both ends (top), every line; closed at one end (bottom), the odd lines only. The stems mark where modes can sit; their heights carry no meaning here.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
Almost an octave deeper
A closed tube fits a wave twice as long. The flute’s lowest mode, \sin(\pi x/L), has room pressure at both ends and swings most in the middle: half a wavelength fits in the tube. The clarinet’s, \cos(\pi x/2L), swings most at the reed and has room pressure at the bell: only a quarter of a wavelength fits. A wave twice as long has half the frequency, so the same ideal tube sounds exactly an octave lower closed at one end.4 Real flutes and clarinets differ a little in length, the clarinet’s mouthpiece and bell change its effective length, and open ends act slightly longer than they are, so the real interval comes out a bit less than an octave.5
4 J. Wolfe, Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets), UNSW: for the same length, the closed pipe’s lowest frequency “c/4L = 140 Hz – one octave lower than the flute”.5 J. Wolfe, Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets), UNSW: the flute’s lowest note is close to middle C, while “the lowest note on a clarinet is either the D or the C# below middle C”; “There are complications due to end corrections”, and the clarinet has a mouthpiece at one end and “a flare and a bell” at the other.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
Blown: one repeating cycle
A blown tube does not ring and fade: the reed or the air jet keeps feeding it, and the air settles into one motion that repeats. The clarinet’s reed acts as a valve: when the pressure in the mouthpiece drops it closes, and when the pressure rises it opens, so the air column drives the reed that feeds it.6 On a flute, a jet of air blown across the embouchure hole does the reed’s job.7 Either way the result is a self-sustained oscillation (appendix), at a playing frequency close to the tube’s sounding mode. For the lowest notes that is c/4L on the clarinet and c/2L on the flute, with L the tube up to the first open hole: the fingers choose the note by choosing L.
6 J. Wolfe, Clarinet acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: “the reed acts like an oscillating valve”.7 J. Wolfe, Flute acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: “The flutist blows a rapid jet of air across the embouchure hole”; “The flute is open at both ends.”8 J. Wolfe, Clarinet acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: “the sound spectrum in the low register has strong first and third harmonics, but weak second and fourth”; even harmonics become more important from about E4.9 J. Wolfe, Clarinet acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: added harmonics make the sound brighter and louder; soft playing in the linear range gives “few high harmonics”.The tube’s modes pick the strong partials. A sound that repeats has partials only at whole-number multiples of its repetition rate (post 1), but it may have all of them. So the clarinet’s modes are odd multiples only, while its sound has even multiples too: weak in the low register, where no mode of the tube supports them, but not absent. In the low register the clarinet has strong first and third harmonics and weak second and fourth; from about E4 up, the even harmonics matter more.8 Blowing harder drives the reed further from gentle, nearly linear motion, which adds high harmonics, so the tone gets brighter as well as louder.9


  
  
  The blown sounds, as multiples of the note being played: the flute (top) has every whole-number multiple; the clarinet (bottom) has strong odd multiples and faint even ones. The demos' sounds are made this way; the exact strengths are an illustrative choice.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
section: Overblowing: a twelfth or an octave
text:
Overblowing: a twelfth or an octave
The flute’s spectrum has every whole-number multiple of its lowest frequency; the clarinet’s has only the odd ones, with nothing in between. So when a clarinetist presses the register key, the tube jumps to its next mode, 3 times its lowest frequency: an octave and a fifth, called a twelfth.10 A flutist overblows with a faster jet, and the flute’s next mode is 2 times its lowest, an octave.11 That is why clarinet fingerings repeat a twelfth apart and flute fingerings an octave apart. (The demo keeps the low-register tone colour when the register key is on.)
10 J. Wolfe, Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets), UNSW: “the second register of the clarinet is a musical twelfth above the first”.11 J. Wolfe, Flute acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: blowing harder or narrowing the lips gives “a faster jet”, and the flute “jumps up” to the octave, 2f_1.


DetailsHow the register key picks out the 3× mode

The register key opens a small hole about a third of the way down the closed part of the tube. An open hole pulls the pressure there toward room pressure, which spoils the fundamental, a mode that needs pressure variation at that point. For one note in the low register the hole sits right where that note’s 3f_1 mode has no pressure variation anyway, so the open hole does not disturb that mode. For the other notes the hole is off that point, and a second effect helps: the air in a small hole has mass, so the faster it must move back and forth, the harder it is to move. At the fundamental’s lower frequency the hole leaks enough to spoil that mode; at the 3f_1 mode’s higher frequency it acts almost as a plug: “high frequency waves pass by as though it were closed”. Either way the tube jumps to the 3f_1 mode. (J. Wolfe, Clarinet acoustics: an introduction, UNSW)


For a sustained instrument the four aspects come from different places than for a ringing one: the repeating cycle gives the whole-number multiples, the tube’s modes set which are strong, and the player sets the rest.


The clarinet’s four aspects, read off its blown sound.


Aspect
Clarinet (and flute)




Pitch
the playing frequency, close to the tube’s sounding mode: c/4L for the clarinet’s lowest notes (c/2L for the flute’s), with L chosen by the fingers; the register key jumps to 3\times (the flute overblows to 2\times)


Loudness
the breath: blowing harder is louder


Timbre
in the low register, strong odd partials and weak even ones, picked by the tube’s modes; more even ones higher up; brighter when played louder


Duration
as long as the player blows

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
The Shape of a Sound · ← 2 · One string, end to end · Violin → · Glossary
Struck or plucked and left to ring, most instruments sound at the frequencies of their own eigenvalues: a little sharp of the whole-number lines on a piano, far off them on a kalimba, between them on a drum. Bowed, blown or, like the theremin, kept going by a circuit, they sound exactly on the lines. Below, one instrument from each of the five Hornbostel–Sachs classes, sorted by what makes the sound,1 plays Grieg,2 every voice built from the spectra on this page.
The reason, in one sentence: a ringing instrument moves as a sum of its own modes, as the string does, so you hear its spectrum; a bowed or blown one is pushed into one repeating cycle, and a repeating cycle has only whole-number partials.

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
The same recipe
Every instrument below is a problem of the same shape as the string’s: an equation, how the object is held, and how it starts or is driven. For the ones left to ring, the string’s argument carries over to every bounded object here: each has its own shapes, the eigenfunctions of its operator, and every motion is a sum of them, each swinging at f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi, apart from the glockenspiel’s two drifts, its slide and tilt, which move as a + bt. The exception is the kettledrum: its sound radiates into the unbounded air around it, which takes it outside this argument (see the fold), so its ratios here are measured.3
3 A kettledrum measured by A. H. Benade, Fundamentals of Musical Acoustics, Oxford University Press, 1976, chapter 9, pp. 143–144, as tabulated by HyperPhysics, The Timpani, Georgia State University: spoke modes at about 1.50, 2.00, 2.49 and 2.98 times the lowest.


PreciselyThe theorem, and its three names uses Hilbert spaces

What carries over from the string: on a bounded object with a reasonable edge, each of these operators is self-adjoint and \geq 0 and has a compact resolvent, so it has an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions, and drifts split off. The three routes are Sturm–Liouville theory for strings and tubes, a compact Green’s operator for bars, and Rellich’s theorem for drums (R. Courant and D. Hilbert, Methods of Mathematical Physics, vol. 1, Interscience, 1953, chapters III (symmetric kernels), V and VI; L. C. Evans, Partial Differential Equations, 2nd ed., American Mathematical Society, 2010, sections 5.7 and 6.5.1). The kettledrum’s radiation, sound carried away into the unbounded air, makes its problem non-self-adjoint, and its full air loading is beyond this page; the air’s added mass alone would keep it inside the theorem, as the drum page’s toy model of the air does.
A Sturm–Liouville problem is -(p\,X')' + q\,X = \lambda\,w\,X on a bounded interval, with p, w > 0 and one condition at each end of the form \alpha X + \beta X' = 0; the string (p = c^2, q = 0, w = 1) and the tubes, open or closed at each end, are of this form, and its eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis (R. Courant and D. Hilbert, Methods of Mathematical Physics, vol. 1, Interscience, 1953, chapters V and VI). For a bar, (A + 1)^{-1} is an integral operator with a kernel continuous on [0, L]^2, the Green’s operator, which is compact and self-adjoint, so the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators applies to it, and its eigenfunctions are A’s. For a drumhead, Rellich’s theorem says that on a bounded region, every sequence of shapes that vanish on the rim and have \iint u^2 and \iint |\nabla u|^2 bounded has a subsequence converging in mean square; this makes (A + 1)^{-1} compact (L. C. Evans, Partial Differential Equations, 2nd ed., American Mathematical Society, 2010, section 5.7). A drift occurs only when A has the eigenvalue 0: on this page, for the glockenspiel bar.

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
Two kinds of entry
A ringing entry is struck or plucked, then left alone: its partials sit wherever its spectrum falls, each fading at its own rate.
A self-sustained entry is kept going by the player, with a bow, an air jet, a reed or an amplifier, whose push depends on the motion itself, not in proportion to it.4 Its motion settles into one repeating cycle, a self-sustained oscillation, so its partials are exact whole-number multiples (post 1), whatever the spectrum of the driven part, the resonator; the drive and the resonator decide only which partials are strong.
4 Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapters 10 (bowed strings), 15 (woodwind reed instruments) and 16 (flutes).In every demo the stems are the sound’s partials on the pitch ruler, taller when stronger, and the picture is slowed down and enlarged.

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A piano
A piano note is clear, but its upper partials run slightly sharp of the whole-number lines, more so the higher they are, because the steel wire resists bending as well as being pulled straight.5 So an exact 2 : 1 octave beats, and tuners widen octaves, most at the keyboard’s ends.6
5 N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 12 (the piano); Wikipedia, Inharmonicity.6 O. L. Railsback, “Scale temperament as applied to piano tuning”, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 9 (1938), 274 (DOI); Wikipedia, Piano acoustics.
  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  Middle C, struck an eighth of the way along (books commonly give 1/7 to 1/9, though on modern pianos many notes are struck nearer the end: Conklin), where the 8th mode stands still, so in the model its stem is zero. Computed: the stem positions, with B = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴, a rough value for a middle C wire. Modelled: each mode starts in proportion to its height under the hammer, with a roll-off for the felt. Illustrative: the fading times.

The spectrum is f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, where B measures the wire’s stiffness, about 4.4\times10^{-4} for a middle C wire. The player controls the hammer’s speed (harder is louder and brighter),7 the dampers and the pedals; none of them moves a frequency (A Piano).
7 D. A. Russell, Hammer nonlinearity, dynamics and the piano sound, 1997: a heavy blow acts as a hard spring, and loud notes are brighter. A. Askenfelt and E. Jansson, “From touch to string vibrations” (the nonlinear hammer), in Five Lectures on the Acoustics of the Piano, Royal Swedish Academy of Music, 1990: the felt stiffens as it is compressed.Deep dive: the piano →

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A kalimba
A kalimba tine gives a click, then a clean note: its first overtone, far off the lines and strong at the attack, dies within a fraction of a second.8 The thumb bends the tine into a smooth curve and lets go.
8 D. M. F. Chapman, The sound of the African thumb piano (kalimba), Acoustics’08 Paris, paper 5aMUf1, Acoustical Society of America, 2008: one dominant overtone, at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, dying away quickly after the attack.
  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  A tine at A4, 440 Hz, pushed at its tip and let go. Computed: the stem positions and each stem's starting height, the push on the bridge (the shear force at the clamp) from the smooth bent start (a cubic, derived on the kalimba page). Illustrative: the fading times, chosen to match Chapman's observation that the overtones die within a fraction of a second; the stems shrink as each partial fades. The tine is drawn as it moves; in displacement its first overtone is only 2.5% of the fundamental, so the picture shows mostly the first mode, while in the push on the bridge it starts at 55%.

The spectrum is in the ratios 1 : 6.27 : 17.55, and f_1 \propto 1/L^2: half the length sounds two octaves up.9 The player sets the loudness by how far the tip is pushed and can stop a tine with a finger; makers tune a tine by sliding it over the bridge.10
9 Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapter 2 (strings and bars).10 Kalimba Magic, on tuning tines.Deep dive: the kalimba →

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A glockenspiel
A glockenspiel gives a bright, clear note although its overtones sit off the lines: they are high and die quickly, leaving the fundamental.11 Its bar is the same kind of steel bar as the kalimba’s tine, with both ends free; it rests on soft supports and is struck with a mallet. 
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2u_{xxxx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 \ \text{ at } x = 0 \text{ and } x = L, \\
u(x, 0) = 0, \qquad u_t(x, 0) = v_0(x).
\end{gathered}
 Here \kappa^2 is the bar’s stiffness over its mass, and v_0 the mallet’s blow (fold).
11 G. P. Scavone, Percussion instruments, course notes, CCRMA, Stanford University, 1999: “All but the lowest transverse mode die out quickly when the bar is struck”; Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 19 (mallet percussion).12 Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapters 2 and 19.The spectrum is in the ratios 1 : 2.756 : 5.404, off the lines, from \cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = 1.12 It also has two eigenvalues 0, the bar sliding or tilting without bending: drifts, which move as a + bt instead of swinging and make no sound.

  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  A bar tuned to C6, 1047 Hz, struck a little off its middle. Computed: the stem positions. Illustrative: the starting strengths and the fading times. The bar is drawn on its two supports, at its fundamental's still points.

The supports, at the fundamental’s still points 0.224L from each end, barely damp it.13 Xylophone and marimba bars, unlike glockenspiel bars, are thinned underneath to put the first overtone on a line, 3× and 4×.14 The player sets the loudness by the blow, the brightness by the mallet, metal brighter and rubber warmer,15 and stops a note with a hand; some glockenspiels on a stand have a damper pedal.16
13 Glockenspiel, PHYS 341 course wiki, University of British Columbia, 2017: supports at the nodes.14 Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 19; Glockenspiel, UBC PHYS 341 course wiki, 2017: glockenspiel bars left uniform.15 Vienna Symphonic Library, Glockenspiel, Academy: hard mallets brighter. K. Peters, How to choose the right mallet, Yamaha Music Educators Hub, 7 May 2019: metal mallets brighter, rubber warmer.16 Vienna Symphonic Library, Glockenspiel, Academy: a damper pedal on stand models, none on table models; notes damped by hand.


DetailsWhere the equation comes from

Here \kappa^2 = EI/\rho S: E is steel’s Young’s modulus, I the second moment of area of the cross-section, \rho the density and S the cross-section’s area; v_0 is the mallet’s blow, concentrated where it lands. The equation is the kalimba tine’s beam equation, from the same slice of bar (derived on the kalimba page). Only the ends differ: on soft supports both ends are free, so at each end no bending moment and no shear force act, u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0. The supports are taken as not holding the bar at all; resting at the fundamental’s still points, they are where that mode does not move.





PreciselyThe spectrum, step by step uses a 2×2 determinant

With \lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4, X = b_1\cos\beta x + b_2\sin\beta x + b_3\cosh\beta x + b_4\sinh\beta x. The free left end, X''(0) = X'''(0) = 0, gives b_3 = b_1 and b_4 = b_2. With c_1 = \cos\beta L, s_1 = \sin\beta L, c_2 = \cosh\beta L and s_2 = \sinh\beta L (hyperbolic functions), the free right end gives (c_2 - c_1)b_1 + (s_2 - s_1)b_2 = 0 and (s_2 + s_1)b_1 + (c_2 - c_1)b_2 = 0, whose determinant is (c_2 - c_1)^2 - (s_2^2 - s_1^2) = 2 - 2c_1c_2. So \cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = 1, with roots \beta L = 4.7300, 7.8532, 10.9956, \dots For \lambda = 0, X'''' = 0 with free ends leaves exactly X = a + bx: two eigenfunctions with eigenvalue 0, whose coordinates move as q = a + bt. The fundamental’s still points, where X_1 = 0, are at 0.224L and 0.776L (computed).

Drums
A bass drum booms with no clear pitch; a kettledrum, one of the timpani, plays a note. Both heads are a stretched skin whose ideal frequencies fall between the lines;17 on the kettledrum the air pulls the spoke modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 times a base, and the round modes radiate away within a fraction of a second.18 Step through it:

The bass drummer strikes slightly off center and shortens the note by muffling the head with a leg or a towel;19 the timpanist strikes between halfway and three-quarters of the way out, and retunes by changing the head’s tension, usually with a pedal.20

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A violin, bowed
A bowed string holds a steady note with its partials exactly on the lines: the bow’s friction grabs the string and lets it slip once per period, so the string repeats one cycle, which Helmholtz watched through a vibration microscope by 1860.21
21 H. Helmholtz, “On the motion of the strings of a violin”, Proceedings of the Philosophical Society of Glasgow 5 (1860–64), 17–21, read 19 December 1860 (archive.org).
  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  Helmholtz motion of an open G string, 196 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, computed for the ideal string, with strength 1/n, without the wooden body. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the string's modes, on every line too. The picture is the sum of the first 40 modes; dashed, the corner's path, two arcs of a parabola.

The string’s own spectrum is post 2’s, f_n = nf_1; the bowed sound’s partials sit on the same lines, partial n pushing the bridge in proportion to 1/n (derived on the violin page). The left hand chooses the length and adds vibrato; the bow’s speed, force and distance from the bridge set the loudness and brightness.22
22 J. Wolfe, Articulation and vibrato on the violin, UNSW: the left hand stops the string and adds vibrato; J. Wolfe, The bowed string, UNSW: bow speed, position and force.Deep dive: the violin →

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A flute
A flute plays a steady note on the lines; with every hole closed and an ever faster airstream, it climbs the harmonic series, 1, 2, 3, 4, … times the lowest.23 It is a tube of air open at both ends, kept going by a jet blown across the embouchure hole.24 An open end holds room pressure, so the tube’s spectrum has the string’s numbers, f_n = nc/2L, on every line.25
23 J. Wolfe, Flute acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: open at both ends; the harmonic series with every hole closed.24 Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, chapter 16 (flutes); Wolfe, Flute acoustics: the jet.25 J. Wolfe, Pipes and harmonics, UNSW: open and closed ends; Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 8 (pipes).
  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  A steady D4, 294 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, all on the lines; their strengths, 1/n², are an illustrative choice. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the open tube's modes, on every line too. Picture: the air in the tube, darker where the pressure is higher, with thin slabs of air that bunch where it is squeezed.

The player chooses the length with the keys, the loudness with the breath, and the register with that faster, narrower airstream.26
26 Wolfe, Flute acoustics: registers.Deep dive: the flute, on the clarinet page →

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A clarinet
A clarinet sounds a hollow note nearly an octave below a flute of the same length. Its tube is closed at the reed, which halves the lowest frequency and leaves only odd multiples of it, so in the low register the odd partials are strong and the even ones weak.27
27 J. Wolfe, Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets), UNSW: a clarinet about an octave below a flute of the same length; J. Wolfe, Clarinet acoustics: an introduction, UNSW: strong odd harmonics in the low register.

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A harmonica
A harmonica reed’s own overtones sit far off the lines, yet its note has partials only on the lines, odd and even both strong. You hear the air, not the reed: the reed lets one identical puff through its slot per cycle, and repeating puffs have only whole-number partials.30

Stems: the sound's partials, at whole-number multiples of the playing frequency, computed from the puff drawn on the right: one puff per cycle, open for about 30% of it, a shape chosen for illustration. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the reed's modes, at 1 and 6.27 times its lowest; the playing frequency sits somewhat below the lowest, drawn here at 1. The reed is drawn in its first mode, and the slot is drawn open only while the tip is above the plate.

The reed’s spectrum is the kalimba tine’s, 1 : 6.27 : 17.55, and it plays somewhat below its lowest mode.31 The breath sets the loudness and the tone while the pitch hardly moves;32 on a diatonic harmonica, reshaping mouth and throat bends a note down between the hole’s two notes, because the hole’s blow and draw reeds both take part.33

title: Other instruments, same recipe
text:
A theremin
A theremin is played without being touched, and its tone glides as the hand moves.34 It makes the tone with electric circuits, each a coil and a capacitor, an LC circuit, whose charge swings like a mass on a spring: 
\ddot q = -\frac{1}{LC}\,q .
 Here q is the charge, L the coil’s inductance and C the capacitance (fold). An amplifier keeps the circuit swinging at a steady size.35
34 Wikipedia, Theremin.35 Wikipedia, Electronic oscillator: an amplifier feeding a tuned circuit in phase, its amplitude limited by a nonlinearity.36 Wikipedia, Theremin: two radio-frequency oscillators below 500 kHz.The spectrum is one frequency, f = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}), a radio frequency below 500 kHz.36 The instrument runs two such circuits, one changed by the player’s hand, and outputs the difference of their frequencies, which is audible (heterodyning).

  
  
  ▶ Playmotion slowed and enlarged
  An idealized sine theremin at A4, 440 Hz: one stem. A real theremin's tone is not a pure sine: it has overtones. No resonator ticks: the circuits' own frequencies are radio frequencies, far beyond this ruler, and the tone you hear is the difference of two of them. Picture: one coil-and-capacitor circuit, its charge sloshing between the plates, slowed to about one swing a second.

Most players set the pitch with the right hand’s distance from one antenna and the loudness with the left hand’s from the other. Leon Theremin invented it in 1920 and patented it in 1928.37
37 Wikipedia, Theremin: the hands; invented 1920, patented 1928.


DetailsWhere the equation comes from

Here q is the charge on the capacitor, L the coil’s inductance and C the capacitance, so the operator is A = 1/LC, one number. Kirchhoff’s voltage law, which balances voltages as Newton’s law balances forces, says that the voltages around a closed loop add to zero. A capacitor holding charge q has the voltage q/C across it; a coil carrying the current I = \dot q has the voltage L\,\dot I. Around the loop, L\,\ddot q + q/C = 0, that is, \ddot q = -q/LC: the coil plays the mass and 1/C the spring’s stiffness. For ideal parts both laws are linear, so no small-motion step is needed.





DetailsHow two radio frequencies make one audible tone

A mixer multiplies the two oscillators’ signals, and \sin(2\pi f_1t)\sin(2\pi f_2t) = \tfrac12\cos(2\pi(f_1 - f_2)t) - \tfrac12\cos(2\pi(f_1 + f_2)t); a filter keeps the difference. With both near a few hundred kilohertz, a hand that changes one circuit’s capacitance by a small fraction moves the difference across the whole audible range. Real theremins’ mixers and circuits add overtones, on the whole-number lines of the difference frequency, since the output repeats at that rate.

title: What you hear
text:
The Shape of a Sound · 2 · One string, end to end → · Glossary
A sound has a clear pitch when its partials, the pure tones it is made of, sit at or very near whole-number multiples of one frequency. A plucked string’s partials do, so it gives a note you could hum; a struck drum’s don’t, so it gives a thud.
The reason, in one sentence: partials on the multiples of one frequency add up to a sound that repeats at that rate, and the ear hears the repetition rate as the pitch, even when no partial sits there. In the demo, the string’s stems sit on the lines, at exactly 1, 2, 3, … times the lowest; the drum’s sit at 1, 1.59, 2.14, 2.30, … times the lowest, and no frequency in the range we hear as pitch fits them all closely. This post explains why that decides between a note and a thud, using no differential equations.

title: What you hear
text:
Four aspects of a sound
We hear four things in a sound: pitch, loudness, timbre and duration. All four are facts about hearing, measured by asking listeners, not mathematics.1
1 B. C. J. Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, 6th ed., Emerald, Bingley, 2012 (reissued by Brill, Leiden, 2013), chapters 4, 6 and 8 (loudness, pitch, timbre); R. Plomp, Aspects of Tone Sensation: A Psychophysical Study, Academic Press, 1976.Sound is the air pressure p(t) at a listener, as a function of time. The simplest sound is a pure tone, the sound of a tuning fork: a pressure swing a\cos(2\pi f t + \varphi) about the average air pressure, with frequency f in hertz (cycles per second), size a, and phase \varphi, which says where in its cycle it starts.
A partial is one pure-tone component of a sound, with its own frequency, size and fading. An instrument left to ring after a pluck or a strike sounds, to a good approximation, a sum of partials: 
p(t) = \sum_k a_k\, e^{-t/\tau_k} \cos(2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k),
 with frequencies f_k, starting sizes a_k, phases \varphi_k and fading times \tau_k: every \tau_k seconds, partial k shrinks by a factor of e \approx 2.7. Each partial comes from one of the instrument’s modes, a shape the object swings in at one frequency, such as a string swinging as one arc, or as two halves in opposite directions; the body and the room pass them on, adding some ringing of their own. Post 2 derives this form for a string, and the appendix When does an equation have a spectrum? in general; what it leaves out, such as breath, is noise.
A harmonic is a partial at a whole-number multiple n f of a base frequency f, the n-th harmonic; a harmonic sound is one whose partials are all harmonics of one base. An overtone is any partial above the lowest, so for a harmonic sound the first overtone is the second harmonic.

Pitch
Pitch is how high or low a sound is heard, measured as the frequency of the pure tone that listeners match it to.2 Pitch that can carry a melody is heard for repetition rates (defined below) from about 30 Hz,3 and for pure tones up to about 4 or 5 kHz, the traditional upper limit.4 Call this the range we hear as pitch.
2 Acoustical Society of America, Standard terminology: pitch, 11.01; Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, 6th ed., 2012, chapter 6, for the definition by matching to a pure tone.3 D. Pressnitzer, R. D. Patterson and K. Krumbholz, The lower limit of melodic pitch, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 109 (2001), 2074–2084.4 A. J. Oxenham, C. Micheyl, M. V. Keebler, A. Loper and S. Santurette, Pitch perception beyond the traditional existence region of pitch, PNAS 108(18) (2011), 7629–7634.

  ▶ Pure tone, 220 Hz▶ Partials at 220, 440, 660, … Hz▶ Pure tone, 440 Hz
  The second sound has ten partials, at 1, 2, …, 10 times 220 Hz, with sizes 1, 1/2, …, 1/10. It sounds richer than the first and just as high, so its pitch is 220 Hz. The third is an octave higher.




Loudness
Loudness is how strong a sound seems. It is set mainly by the sound pressure level: 10 dB more is ten times the power and sounds about twice as loud.5 It also depends on frequency: at the same level, a low tone sounds quieter than a mid-range one.6
5 S. S. Stevens, “On the psychophysical law”, Psychological Review 64 (1957), 153–181; Wikipedia, Sone (twice as loud per 10 dB) and Stevens’s power law.6 ISO 226:2023, Acoustics — Normal equal-loudness-level contours; HyperPhysics, Equal loudness curves.


DetailsDecibels, equal-loudness contours and the power law

The sound pressure level is 20\log_{10}(p_{\mathrm{rms}}/20\,\mu\mathrm{Pa}) decibels (dB), with p_{\mathrm{rms}} the root-mean-square pressure, the square root of the average squared pressure swing; the intensity, the power carried through each square metre, grows as p_{\mathrm{rms}}^2, so 10 dB more is ten times the intensity. By the equal-loudness contours of ISO 226, which give the level at which pure tones of each frequency sound equally loud to young listeners, a 100 Hz tone needs about 79 dB to match a 1 kHz tone at 60 dB (ISO 226:2023, Acoustics — Normal equal-loudness-level contours; the level is computed from the formula of the 2003 edition, from which the 2023 values differ by at most 0.6 dB, as the standard’s foreword states). At equal intensity, partials spread beyond a certain width in frequency sound louder than partials bunched together (E. Zwicker, G. Flottorp and S. S. Stevens, “Critical band width in loudness summation”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 29 (1957), 548–557). Loudness grows roughly as the 0.3 power of intensity, so 10 dB more sounds about twice as loud, since 10^{0.3} \approx 2 (S. S. Stevens, “On the psychophysical law”, Psychological Review 64 (1957), 153–181; Wikipedia, Stevens’s power law).




  Same size of pressure swing:▶ 100 Hz▶ 1000 Hz▶ 3000 Hz▶ All three in turn
  1000 Hz, three levels:▶ 0, then −10, then −20 dB
  First row: three pure tones with exactly the same size of pressure swing in the signal. With good headphones the 100 Hz tone sounds much quieter than the other two; that is the ear's equal-loudness contour. Small laptop and phone speakers play 100 Hz weakly, which exaggerates the effect, and the level at your ear depends on your volume setting, so the numbers in the text apply only roughly. Second row: one tone, stepped down by 10 dB twice; each step sounds about half as loud.




Timbre
Timbre is what tells apart two sounds of the same loudness and pitch.7 It is mostly the partials’ sizes and how they change, the start especially.8 It also includes how far the partials sit from whole-number multiples, how the sound starts and fades (attack and decay), noise and transients that are not modes (bow noise, breath, hammer thump), and fixed resonances that stay put whatever note is played (formants: a violin’s body, a clarinet’s tone-hole cutoff).9
7 The ANSI/ASA definition of timbre (terminology 12.09), as quoted by Wikipedia, Timbre.8 Wikipedia, Timbre; Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, 6th ed., 2012, chapter 8.9 M. Schleske, Introduction to violin acoustics: sound, on the violin body’s fixed resonances; E. Moers and J. Kergomard, “On the cutoff frequency of clarinet-like instruments. Geometrical versus acoustical regularity”, Acta Acustica united with Acustica 97 (2011), 984–996 (arXiv:1101.4742), and J. Wolfe and colleagues, Clarinet acoustics: F3, UNSW, on the clarinet’s tone-hole cutoff.


DetailsThe evidence, and the formants

Removing the onsets of recorded instrument tones cut listeners’ accuracy at naming the instruments by about 15 percentage points (E. Saldanha and J. F. Corso, “Timbre cues and the identification of musical instruments”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 36 (1964), 2021–2026, as summarized in K. Siedenburg, Specifying the perceptual relevance of onset transients for musical instrument identification, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 145 (2019), 1078–1087). Listeners also hear a finger hitting a piano key and the key hitting bottom (W. Goebl, R. Bresin and I. Fujinaga, Perception of touch quality in piano tones, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 136 (2014), 2839–2850). A violin’s body favors certain bands of frequency whatever the note, as a voice’s formants do (M. Schleske, Introduction to violin acoustics: sound). Above a cutoff frequency, roughly 1 to 1.5 kHz on a clarinet, sound waves travel on past the open tone holes instead of being turned back by them, and that cutoff depends little on the fingering (E. Moers and J. Kergomard, “On the cutoff frequency of clarinet-like instruments. Geometrical versus acoustical regularity”, Acta Acustica united with Acustica 97 (2011), 984–996, arXiv:1101.4742; J. Wolfe and colleagues, Clarinet acoustics: F3, UNSW, on waves passing an open tone hole more easily at higher frequencies).




  ▶ Pure tone▶ Every harmonic▶ Odd harmonics only▶ Every harmonic, plucked
  Four sounds with the same pitch, 220 Hz. The first three are steady and have the same power, which makes them roughly, not exactly, equally loud: one partial; twelve harmonics with sizes 1, 1/2, 1/3, …; and the odd ones of those, which sounds hollow, like a clarinet. The fourth has the second's partials but starts suddenly and fades, the higher partials faster, like a pluck.




Duration
Duration is how long a note sounds. A ringing instrument’s note lasts as long as its fading times allow, unless the player damps it: a key released, a mute, or a hand on the head; a bass drummer stops a note with a leg or a towel on the head.10 A bowed or blown note lasts as long as the player keeps going. How a note fades is part of its timbre; how long it lasts is its duration.
10 “How to play the bass drum properly”, with Keith Aleo, Interlochen Center for the Arts, 3 April 2023.

  Plucked:▶ Let it ring▶ Damp it after 0.35 s
  Bowed:▶ Half a second▶ Two seconds
  A string at 196 Hz. Plucked, it fades on its own unless damped; the damped note has the same partials, all made to die within about a tenth of a second. Bowed, it is a steady tone (partials 1, 1/2, 1/3, … of a repeating motion) that lasts as long as the bow moves.


For an instrument left to ring, all four are heard from three things about its partials: where they sit, how strong they are and how fast they fade. Pitch is heard mainly from where they sit; loudness from their strengths, weighted by frequency; timbre from all three, especially early on, plus sounds such as breath or bow noise; duration from the fading and from when the player stops or damps the note. Bowed and blown notes are different (route 4 below). The rest of this post asks where the partials must sit for a clear pitch.

title: What you hear
text:
Why whole numbers repeat
Two pure tones repeat together only when their frequency ratio is a fraction. Take 220 Hz and 330 Hz, in the ratio 3 : 2: after two cycles of the lower tone the upper one has completed three, so the sum begins again, 110 times a second. In general, for a ratio j/k in lowest terms, the sum repeats every k cycles of the lower tone, at the rate f_1/k. At 1.59 : 1, which is 159/100, that takes 100 cycles: 2.2 times a second for a lower tone at 220 Hz, far below the pitch range.


  ▶ 2 : 1▶ 3 : 2▶ 1.59 : 1 (a drum)Play the slider's ratio
  Ratio2.00×
  
  
  Two pure tones, the lower at 220 Hz. Gray ticks mark cycles of the lower tone. At 2 : 1 the sum repeats every cycle; at 3 : 2 every two; at 1.59 : 1 it lines up only after 100 cycles, far off the right of this picture.


The same holds for any number of steady partials: their sum repeats exactly when all their frequencies are whole-number multiples of one frequency, and then it repeats at the largest such frequency. A signal p is periodic with period P > 0 if p(t+P) = p(t) for every t, and the repetition rate of a sound whose partials are steady and exact whole-number multiples of a common frequency is 1 over its shortest period, which is that largest common frequency. That the sum repeats only for fractions needs one more fact, that sinusoids of different frequencies cannot cancel one another.

Precisely. Let 
p(t) = a_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k\cos(2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k),
 with distinct frequencies f_k > 0 and sizes a_k \ne 0. A time P > 0 is a period of p exactly when every f_k is a whole-number multiple of 1/P. So p is periodic exactly when every ratio f_k/f_1 is a fraction, and then its shortest period is 1/g, where g is the largest frequency of which every f_k is a whole-number multiple.




ProofSinusoids of different frequencies are independent, so a period must fit every partial integrals of products of cosines, and divisibility

Lemma. Let 0 < g_1 < \dots < g_m, and suppose that c + \sum_{j=1}^m \big(\alpha_j\cos(2\pi g_j t) + \beta_j\sin(2\pi g_j t)\big) = 0 for every t. Then c = 0 and every \alpha_j and \beta_j is 0.
Proof of the lemma. For a function h, write \langle h\rangle = \lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T} h(t)\,dt for its long-run average, when the limit exists. For \gamma \ne 0, \int_{-T}^{T}\cos(2\pi\gamma t)\,dt = \sin(2\pi\gamma T)/(\pi\gamma) stays bounded as T grows, so \langle\cos(2\pi\gamma t)\rangle = 0; and \langle 1\rangle = 1. The product formulas 2\cos x\cos y = \cos(x-y) + \cos(x+y) and 2\sin x\sin y = \cos(x-y) - \cos(x+y) then give, for a, b > 0, \langle\cos(2\pi a t)\cos(2\pi b t)\rangle = \langle\sin(2\pi a t)\sin(2\pi b t)\rangle = \tfrac12 if a = b and 0 if a \ne b. A product of a sine and a cosine is an odd function, so its integral over [-T, T] is 0, and so is its average. Multiply the assumed identity by \cos(2\pi g_j t) and average: every term vanishes except \alpha_j/2, by the averages just computed, so \alpha_j = 0. Multiplying by \sin(2\pi g_j t) gives \beta_j = 0 in the same way. What remains is c = 0.
Proof of the statement. If every f_kP is a whole number, each cosine completes whole cycles in time P, so p(t + P) = p(t). Conversely, suppose p(t+P) = p(t) for every t, and write \theta_k = 2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k and \delta_k = 2\pi f_k P. By the identity \cos(\theta + \delta) - \cos\theta = -2\sin(\delta/2)\sin(\theta + \delta/2), 
0 = p(t+P) - p(t) = \sum_{k=1}^n -2a_k\sin(\pi f_kP)\,\sin\!\big(2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k + \pi f_kP\big).
 Expanding each term into \alpha_k\cos(2\pi f_k t) + \beta_k\sin(2\pi f_k t) gives \alpha_k^2 + \beta_k^2 = 4a_k^2\sin^2(\pi f_kP). The lemma, with c = 0, makes every \alpha_k and \beta_k zero, so a_k\sin(\pi f_kP) = 0; since a_k \ne 0 by hypothesis, \sin(\pi f_k P) = 0, which means f_kP is a whole number. This proves the first sentence.
The shortest period. If p has a period P, the first sentence makes every f_kP a whole number, so f_k/f_1 = (f_kP)/(f_1P) is a fraction. Conversely, suppose every f_k/f_1 is a fraction. Over a common denominator N, f_k = n_k h with h = f_1/N and whole numbers n_k. Let d be the greatest common divisor of n_1, \dots, n_n and g = dh; then f_k = m_kg with whole numbers m_k = n_k/d whose greatest common divisor is 1. By the first sentence, P is a period exactly when every m_k\,gP is a whole number. If gP is a whole number, so is every m_k\,gP. Conversely, Bézout’s identity (whole numbers whose greatest common divisor is 1 have a combination with whole-number coefficients equal to 1) gives whole numbers u_k with \sum_k u_km_k = 1, so gP = \sum_k u_k\,(m_k\,gP) is a whole number. So the periods are exactly the whole-number multiples of 1/g, and the shortest is 1/g. Finally, if every f_k is a whole-number multiple of some g', then 1/g' is a period, hence a multiple of 1/g, so g' \le g: g is the largest such frequency.
Check on the examples. Partials at 440, 660 and 880 Hz have h = 220, n_k = 2, 3, 4, d = 1, so g = 220 Hz although no partial sits there. Tones at 100 and 159 Hz have g = 1 Hz: the sum repeats once a second.


For real instruments, whose partials fade or sit only near the multiples, the repetition rate is the largest frequency in the range we hear as pitch that the partials fit within a stated tolerance. A sound that fades cannot repeat exactly, but it can nearly: if every partial sits on a multiple of g and fades with the same time \tau, each period is the one before shrunk by the factor e^{-1/(g\tau)}, by 0.45% at g = 220 Hz and \tau = 1 s. How near the multiples is near enough is a fact about hearing: a low partial mistuned by more than about 1 to 3%, depending on the listener, stands out as a separate tone.11 Within 2%, the middle of that range, the lowest strong partials of the drum in the first demo fit no frequency above about 20 Hz, below the pitch range; the string’s fit 196 Hz exactly.
11 B. C. J. Moore, B. R. Glasberg and R. W. Peters, Thresholds for hearing mistuned partials as separate tones in harmonic complexes, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 80 (1986), 479–483; Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, 6th ed., 2012, chapter 3, on hearing out partials.


PreciselyHow the drum fails to fit, at different tolerances

Take the partials of the drum in the first demo up to 3.2 times the lowest that start with at least a tenth of the strongest one’s size: 1, 1.593, 2.295, 2.653 and 3.155 times 140 Hz. (Its partials at 2.136 and 2.917 start with only about 2% of the strongest’s size, because the strike point or the listening point sits near a still line of their modes.) Call a frequency g a fit within a tolerance \epsilon if each partial lies within the fraction \epsilon of a whole-number multiple ng with n \ge 1. A computer search over g gives the largest fit; adding the drum’s higher partials could only lower it.



Tolerance
Largest fit g




1%

2%

3%

Why a fading sound cannot repeat exactly. If p(t+P) = p(t) for every t, then p(t) = p(t + mP) for every whole number m, and for a sound that dies away this tends to 0 as m grows, so p is zero. A piano’s partials, slightly sharp of the lines, also nearly repeat.
Within 3%, a base of about 46 Hz fits as its 3rd, 5th, 7th, 8th and 10th multiples, each off by up to 3%, with nothing at the base or at its 2nd or 4th multiple. The 3% figure is generous. It comes from a different measurement by the same authors: in an earlier study, a single mistuned low partial of an otherwise exact harmonic sound kept counting fully toward its pitch up to about 3% (B. C. J. Moore, B. R. Glasberg and R. W. Peters, “Relative dominance of individual partials in determining the pitch of complex tones”, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 77 (1985), 1853–1860, as summarized in C. J. Darwin, A. Buffa and R. L. H. M. Smits, Pitch of simultaneous complex sounds with a single mistuned component, Proc. Inst. Acoust. 12, Part 10 (1990), 499–505), whereas the 1 to 3% above is where a partial starts to be heard out on its own (their 1986 study), and here every partial is off at once. What the ear makes of such a sound is a question about hearing; in the first demo, it is a thud.

title: What you hear
text:
The missing fundamental
For a single tone, the ear hears the repetition rate as the pitch, even when no partial sits at it.12 Play the note, then the same note without its 220 Hz partial, and watch the wave.
12 Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, 6th ed., 2012, chapter 6: for a single tone whose prominent partials lie near a harmonic series in the pitch range, the pitch is close to that series’ base, even when its own partial is missing.

  
    ▶ The note▶ Without its 220 Hz partial
    Play again
  
  
  
  
  Mix your own
    Pure toneHollow, like a clarinet
    
  
  The wave over three cycles of 220 Hz; gray ticks mark each 1/220 of a second. Stems: how strong each partial is, at 1, 2, 3, … times 220 Hz, on the pitch ruler. The readout gives the repetition rate, the largest frequency of which every partial present is a whole-number multiple.


The wave changes shape but still repeats every 1/220 of a second, since 440, 660, 880, … Hz are all multiples of 220 Hz, and the pitch stays. Hearing the pitch without its fundamental is the missing-fundamental effect; it keeps a deep voice’s pitch over a telephone that carries little below about 300 Hz.13 Keep only 2×, 4×, 6× and 8× in “Mix your own”, and the pitch jumps an octave.
13 Wikipedia, Missing fundamental.
Beats
Two close partials fit no series in the pitch range, and the ear hears one tone that swells and fades. For two pure tones of equal size, the sum-to-product formula gives 
\cos(2\pi f_1 t) + \cos(2\pi f_2 t) = 2\cos\big(\pi (f_2 - f_1) t\big)\,\cos\big(\pi (f_1 + f_2) t\big),
 a tone at the average frequency whose size swells and fades |f_2 - f_1| times a second: beats.14 Tones at 220 and 222 Hz repeat together exactly twice a second, far below the pitch range; you hear a 221 Hz tone wobbling twice a second. Faster beats sound rough, and tones far enough apart sound as two smooth tones.15
14 Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing, 6th ed., 2012, chapter 1.15 R. Plomp and W. J. M. Levelt, Tonal consonance and critical bandwidth, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 38 (1965), 548–560.

  ▶ 220 + 222 Hz▶ 220 + 228 Hz▶ 220 + 245 Hz▶ 220 + 330 Hz
  
  
  The sum of two equal pure tones over one second. Its outline swells and shrinks as many times a second as the two frequencies differ: 2, 8 and 25 times; at 110 Hz apart the swells come too fast to see here, and you hear two smooth tones.




Exceptions to the pitch rule
Three kinds of sound break the rule.
Chords. The ear sorts the partials into several series and hears several pitches. C4 and G4 tuned to an exact 3 : 2 have all their partials on multiples of 130.8 Hz (C3), so together they repeat 130.8 times a second; yet you hear two notes, because the ear hears two sets of harmonics with different bases as two sounds.16
16 A. S. Bregman, Auditory Scene Analysis: The Perceptual Organization of Sound, MIT Press, 1990; and his page Introduction to auditory scene analysis.

  ▶ C4▶ G4▶ C4 and G4 together▶ C3, the pair's repetition rate
  Each note has eight harmonics, with sizes 1, 1/2, …, 1/8: C4 at 261.6 Hz, G4 at exactly 3/2 of that, 392.4 Hz. Together they repeat 130.8 times a second, the rate of the last sound, which is not what the pair sounds like.


Bells and kettledrums. A harmonic subset of the partials sets the pitch, and the ear may choose an octave above the base. A bell is heard roughly an octave below its main partial, the nominal, often with no partial at the pitch heard.17 A kettledrum is named an octave above the base its main partials fit.18 The fold gives the partials; the drums in post 3 give the kettledrum’s modes.
17 W. A. Hibbert, What note do we hear when a bell rings?18 HyperPhysics, The Timpani, tabulating A. H. Benade, Fundamentals of Musical Acoustics, Oxford University Press, 1976.19 J. Jaatinen and J. Pätynen, Effect of inharmonicity on pitch perception and subjective tuning of piano tones, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 152 (2022), 1146–1157.20 Moore, Glasberg and Peters, Thresholds for hearing mistuned partials as separate tones in harmonic complexes, 1986.Strongly stretched partials. Partials running sharp of the lines, as on a stiff piano string, pull the pitch up;19 beyond the tolerance above, a partial is heard out on its own.20



DetailsThe bell’s and the kettledrum’s partials

The bell. In a well-tuned church bell the main partials, the hum, prime, tierce, quint and nominal, sit near 0.5, 1, 1.2, 1.5 and 2 times the prime, and two more, the superquint and the octave nominal, near 3 and 4 times (W. A. Hibbert, The upper partials of bells). The strike note, the pitch the bell is heard at, is close to the prime (Wikipedia, Strike tone). The nominal, superquint and octave nominal, nearly in the ratios 2 : 3 : 4, are heard as harmonics of a missing fundamental, the strike note, which lies roughly an octave below the nominal (W. A. Hibbert, The strike note of bells, first published in The Ringing World, 20 June 2003, p. 586). It can differ from half the nominal by about a quarter of a semitone, and often no partial sits exactly at it, a puzzle Rayleigh noted in 1890; which partials set the note also depends on the bell’s size (W. A. Hibbert, What note do we hear when a bell rings?). Measured from the hum, the main partials sit at 1, 2, 2.4, 3, 4, 6 and 8: whole numbers, except the tierce, a minor third above the prime. Without the tierce, the main partials fit the hum as base, yet the bell is heard an octave higher.
The kettledrum. A kettledrum’s air pulls one set of its modes near 2, 3, 4 and 5 times a base, yet players name the note an octave higher, at the lowest of the set, the drum’s principal tone. A kettledrum measured by Benade, tuned to C3, had its principal tone at 130.8 Hz and partials at about 1.50, 2.00, 2.49 and 2.98 times it, close to 3, 4, 5 and 6 times half of it, together with others off this pattern (HyperPhysics, The Timpani, tabulating A. H. Benade, Fundamentals of Musical Acoustics, Oxford University Press, 1976). On C2, 65.4 Hz, that set forms a near-harmonic series, and HyperPhysics notes that the missing-fundamental effect might then give the pitch C2; the drum is named for its principal tone, C3. Vienna’s Institute of Musical Acoustics names the principal tone (“Grundton”) as the mode with one still line through the center, and notes that the drum’s many partials off whole-number ratios make its exact pitch hard to pin down (Institute of Musical Acoustics (Wiener Klangstil), University of Music and Performing Arts Vienna, The Viennese timpani).

title: What you hear
section: Four routes to a clear pitch
text:
Four routes to a clear pitch
Instruments reach a clear pitch by four routes: modes on the whole numbers by nature, modes moved there by design, off-line partials suppressed, or a drive that repeats.
1×2×3×

By nature: strings and air columns. A string’s n-th mode fits n half-waves between its ends (the picture), and every wave travels along the string at the same speed, so an ideal string’s n-th mode swings at exactly n times the lowest frequency. A flute’s air column, open at both ends, resonates at every whole-number multiple, and a clarinet’s, closed at the reed, at the odd ones.21 Guitars and harps take this route, and the piano nearly, since stiffness pushes its partials slightly sharp. Bowed strings and winds start here too; route 4 makes their partials exact.
By design. A kettledrum’s air slows its coarse shapes most, pulling one set of modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 (the drums in post 3). A marimba bar’s arch, cut underneath, moves its first overtone from 2.76 times the lowest, for a uniform bar, to 4 times; a xylophone’s shallower cut, to 3 times.22 A patch of paste loading the middle of a tabla’s head brings its modes near whole-number ratios.23 Founders shape and tune a bell so that most of its principal partials sit on multiples of half the strike note, all but the minor-third tierce.24
By suppression. Some off-line partials are weak or die fast: a kalimba tine’s overtones, at 6.27 and 17.55 times its lowest, die within a fraction of a second,25 and a struck glockenspiel bar’s modes all die out quickly except the lowest.26 Others are never started: a strike at a still point of a mode does not set that mode going, and timpanists strike between halfway and three-quarters of the way out,27 near the still lines of several modes that do not fit the note.
By a periodic drive: bow and breath. A bow or a breath keeps feeding the motion, which settles into a single repeating cycle, so its partials sit at exact whole-number multiples, whatever the object’s own modes:28 a bow’s stick and slip drive all of a string’s resonances at exactly harmonic ratios, and a harmonica reed, whose own overtones are off the lines, chops the air into identical puffs (the harmonica in post 3). The resonator’s modes only shape which partials are strong, and the player sets loudness and duration.

21 J. Wolfe, Open vs closed pipes (flutes vs clarinets), UNSW.22 HyperPhysics, Xylophone and marimba; G. P. Scavone, Percussion instruments, course notes, CCRMA, Stanford University, 1999; N. H. Fletcher and T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer, 1998, chapter 19 (bars).23 C. V. Raman and S. Kumar, “Musical drums with harmonic overtones”, Nature 104 (1920), 500.24 W. A. Hibbert, The upper partials of bells; Wikipedia, Strike tone.25 D. M. F. Chapman, The sound of the African thumb piano (kalimba), Acoustics’08 Paris, paper 5aMUf1, Acoustical Society of America, 2008.26 G. P. Scavone, Percussion instruments, CCRMA, Stanford University, 1999 (the glockenspiel).27 HyperPhysics, The Timpani (the playing spot).28 J. Wolfe, How harmonic are harmonics?, UNSW. Why whole numbers repeat proves this for a finite sum of partials.

  1 · By nature:▶ Plucked string
  2 · By design:▶ Uniform bar▶ Undercut bar
  3 · Suppressed:▶ Kalimba tine▶ The same, overtones ringing as long
  4 · Driven:▶ Harmonica reed, plucked▶ The same reed, blown
  Row 2: a bar's lowest two partials at middle C, with the overtone at 2.76 times the lowest (a uniform bar) or at 4 times (an undercut marimba bar); sizes and fading times illustrative. Row 3: a kalimba tine at C5, its overtones at 6.27 and 17.55 times the lowest, fading fast as measured, then the same partials made to ring as long as the lowest. Row 4: the reed has the tine's frequencies when plucked; blown, it sounds a steady tone with partials at whole-number multiples only.


Why does a vibrating object have modes at all, and why do their frequencies form a list? For the string, post 2 answers this completely; the appendix When does an equation have a spectrum? answers it in general.

title: What you hear
text:
Dynamics change timbre too
A harder blow sounds louder and brighter. A piano hammer’s felt gets harder the more it is squashed, so a fast hammer stays on the string for a shorter time and starts more high partials;29 with a felt that stayed equally soft, a loud note would be a soft note turned up.30 The piano in post 3 takes it up.
29 A. Askenfelt and E. Jansson, “From touch to string vibrations” (the nonlinear hammer; string contact), in Five Lectures on the Acoustics of the Piano, Royal Swedish Academy of Music, 1990.30 D. A. Russell, Hammer nonlinearity, dynamics and the piano sound, 1997.

  ▶ Soft blow▶ Hard blow▶ Soft blow, turned up
  Middle C on a model piano string. The hard blow has stronger high partials and an average level 10 dB higher; the third button plays the soft blow 10 dB louder, at the hard blow's average level, and it still sounds duller. How fast the partials fall off with number is an illustrative choice, not computed from a model of the felt.
